entry.title: Extending Keccak's 2011 second-preimage observation to new bridge constructions and protocol designs (cryptanalysis paper)
entry.summary: Beyond the Event Horizon of Keccak, Extending the Observation from 2011 and applications IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026 The paper extends a 2011 observation about the Keccak sponge, showing that a path from an all-zero-capacity state back to such a state yields an infinite family of second preimages for any message of at least one full rate block. It gives three new theorems covering arbitrary capacity values via two-block loops, k-block loops and capacity-map cycles, and a bridge method that yields 2^k multicollisions, with verified full-round examples on Keccak-f[200] and Keccak-f[1600] with c=32. It also proposes protocols that exploit the asymmetry between minting and forging Keccak bridges, whose end-to-end security is stated to remain open.

entry.title: Shor's algorithm on cat qubits: estimated resources to factor RSA-2048
entry.summary: Shor's algorithm compiled on cat qubits: 22 593 qubits for RSA-2048 in 3.14 days IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026 This paper presents an end-to-end resource estimate of Shor's algorithm on superconducting cat qubits, covering RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP. It compiles the main subroutines to physical-qubit operations on repetition-cat-code and LDPC-cat-code architectures and proposes chip layouts and schedules. Under stated assumptions, factoring RSA-2048 is estimated to require about 23,000 cat qubits and 3.14 days, while solving ECDLP on secp256k1 needs at most 30,000 cat qubits and 1 hour.

entry.title: Barriers to Identity-Based Encryption in Generic Group-Action Models
entry.summary: Barriers to Identity-Based Encryption in Generic Group-Action Models IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies whether identity-based encryption (IBE) can be built from the basic interface of generic cryptographic group actions. In the type-safe generic group-action model, the authors prove that an IBE scheme whose public parameters contain n non-origin action-set element-handles can support at most n identities, and they show a matching construction that makes this bound tight. The result is extended to random-representation models and to actions with an inversion-like twist, suggesting IBE may require extra algebraic structure or non-black-box techniques.

entry.title: Efficient SIMD SHAKE via Cost-Aware Permutation Scheduling (a method for scheduling hash computations more efficiently in parallel)
entry.summary: Efficient SIMD SHAKE through Cost-Aware Permutation Scheduling IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026 The paper presents a cost-aware method for scheduling Keccak permutations across multiple hash streams during a single cryptographic algorithm execution. It groups ready streams and splits long streams into segments for regrouping, guided by a cost model covering permutation calls, state movement, initialization, and input preparation. The method is evaluated on ML-KEM and HAETAE across Apple M5, Cortex-A72, and Intel Core i5-11500 processors. Reported speedups reach 1.31x for ML-KEM encapsulation, 1.44x for decapsulation, 1.28x for HAETAE signing, and 1.26x for verification.

entry.title: Private information retrieval analyzed through probabilistic inference
entry.summary: PIR through the Lens of Probabilistic Inference IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026 Private Information Retrieval (PIR) lets a client fetch a database entry without servers learning which index was requested. The paper shows that each server's computation in classic PIR protocols amounts to computing a marginal probability of a product distribution, so efficient exact inference algorithms yield faster server computation. It gives improved server algorithms for several structured function classes and, under the randomized Circuit Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, proves that substantially sublinear server computation cannot be achieved uniformly for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits.

entry.title: Faster complete formulas and their application to curves with efficient endomorphisms
entry.summary: Faster complete formulas and their application to curves with efficient endomorphisms IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026 The paper revisits scalar multiplication on prime curves y² = x³ + b with p ≡ 1 (mod 3), a family that includes secp256k1, BN, and BLS curves. It applies a 15-year-old technique in a new way to reduce the best complete addition from 12 to 11 multiplications. Implemented in libsecp256k1, this yields a 5.2% improvement in constant-time fixed-base scalar multiplication.

entry.title: An algebraic data structure for fast polynomial evaluation over large-characteristic fields
entry.summary: An Algebraic Polynomial Evaluation Datastructure for Fields of Large Characteristic IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026 This paper studies data structures that evaluate a multivariate polynomial at any input point by using random access to a precomputed encoding of the polynomial. The authors construct algebraic curves over prime fields by using the base-β representation of prime field elements, reducing evaluation recursively to points in boxes of decreasing size. The resulting structure greatly improves the dependence of query complexity on the characteristic p and removes p from the data structure size. The variant of the results is enough to disprove Miltersen's conjecture for all finite fields.

entry.title: Quantum sensors for measuring chip electromagnetic leakage in side-channel attacks
entry.summary: Towards Quantum Sensing for Side-Channel Analysis IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies how quantum sensing based on nitrogen-vacancy centers can analyze the dynamic electromagnetic fields of integrated circuits for side-channel analysis. The authors build a radio-frequency spectrometer with a 1.1 GHz real-time bandwidth that probes the frequency spectrum directly, without Fourier transforms or frequency sweeps. They use it to analyze electromagnetic emanations from an RSA decryption and to detect leakage in a Number Theoretic Transform implementation running on a Cortex M4 microcontroller.

entry.title: Radical isogeny computation on curves in many models
entry.summary: Radical isogenies on every model IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies radical isogeny formulae, which compute a cyclic chain of N-isogenies using one N-th root per step without sampling torsion points. Previously, such formulae for general N were known only in Tate normal form. The authors give radical steps of odd degree N on many curve models, including Montgomery and twisted Edwards curves, and report exact operation counts for each model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend radical isogeny formulas from Tate normal form to many curve models, giving explicit steps for each odd degree with exact operation counts and reported costs.

entry.title: "Tractable, Not Truncated": Security Analysis of Colored-Noise True Random Number Generators via Fractional Brownian Motion
entry.summary: Tractable, Not Truncated: Colored-Noise TRNG Security via Fractional Brownian Motion IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026 This paper examines oscillator-based true random number generators, whose randomness comes from thermal and flicker noise. It argues that existing models discard or truncate flicker noise's long memory, which overstates security. The authors model oscillator phase with fractional Brownian motion, prove a quasi-renewal property, and derive closed-form worst-case min-entropy and sampling requirements. Experiments on FPGA and ASIC platforms show flicker noise dominates, and including it can raise bitrate by two to three orders of magnitude.

entry.title: Quantum lower bounds for multi-collisions in bounded-type functions
entry.summary: Quantum Multi-Collision Lower Bounds for Arbitrary Bounded Types IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies quantum collision finding for functions of a prescribed exact type. The authors prove that finding r-collisions across ℓ distinct equality classes has worst-case bounded-error quantum query complexity Θ_{k,r}(ℓ^{2^{r-1}/(2^r-1)} N^{(2^{r-1}-1)/(2^r-1)}), uniformly over all feasible alphabet sizes q≥n. The proof uses the compressed permutation oracle and extends to arbitrary exact types with bounded class sizes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors analyze quantum multi-collision query lower bounds using compressed permutation oracles, extend them to arbitrary bounded types, and report the same exponent via Belovs's transfer framewor

entry.title: Rerandomizable Garbling Beyond BHHO-KMHE, with a Lattice-Based Construction
entry.summary: Rerandomizable Garbling Beyond BHHO-KMHE and a Construction from LWE IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies rerandomizable garbling schemes (RGS), a basic building block for advanced cryptographic constructions such as multi-hop homomorphic encryption and iO combiners. All previously known RGS rely on discrete-logarithm-type assumptions. The authors introduce a new garbling technique that moves the job of hiding homomorphic transformations from the encryption scheme to the garbling itself, allowing RGS to be built from key-and-message homomorphic encryption with weaker properties. They also give an LWE-based KMHE instantiation, a variant of the GSW fully homomorphic encryption scheme, yielding the first RGS construction that does not rely on discrete-logarithm assumptions and may be post-quantum secure.

entry.title: OblivDGL: A Practical Privacy-Preserving Deep Graph Learning Framework
entry.summary: OblivDGL: Oblivious Deep Graph Learning Made Practical IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents OblivDGL, a framework for secure graph neural network (GNN) inference and training that protects both graph data and models. Inspired by the Deep Graph Library (DGL), it introduces an oblivious message passing paradigm and an encrypted graph representation built on function secret sharing (FSS). According to the authors' evaluations on four benchmark graph datasets, OblivDGL cuts communication cost by up to 1024x and speeds up secure training by up to 14.3x compared with prior secure GNN frameworks, while inference achieves up to 754x lower communication and a 4.19x speedup.

entry.title: Recovering Falcon Private Keys by Combining Sampler Side-Channel Leakages
entry.summary: Falcon Key Recovery from Joint Sampler Leakages IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 Falcon and the FN-DSA standard based on it create signatures using discrete Gaussian sampling, and power consumption during this step leaks information about secret-dependent values. The paper presents a key-recovery method that combines three observations from each sampler call and turns the resulting candidate sets into constraints on the secret key, solved by regression and integer reconstruction without lattice reduction like LLL or BKZ. The attack recovers all 50 evaluation keys on PQClean Falcon-512 and still recovers 38 of 50 keys on c-fn-dsa, showing that instruction-level normalization alone is insufficient. ★★★★★ Notable: Fuses three sampler side-channel observations to recover Falcon keys without LLL/BKZ; the abstract reports recovering all 50 evaluation keys on Cortex-M4 with a median of 11 signatures.

entry.title: Poly2MsgLeaks: Certified Key Recovery via Polynomial-to-Message Power Leakage
entry.summary: Poly2MsgLeaks: Certified Key Recovery from Polynomial-to-Message Leakage IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents Poly2MsgLeaks, a profiled chosen-ciphertext power-analysis attack that recovers the full 512-coefficient secret key of the SMAUG-T public-key encryption scheme in its TiMER parameter set. Using six physical polynomial-to-message traces recorded on an STM32F415, the attack recovers 999 of 1,000 unseen secrets, and recovers all 1,000 secrets of a second cohort at a mean cost of 7.021 traces without false acceptances. Against single-write message assembly and a two-share masked P2M implementation, the evaluated six-execution attack recovers no complete secret. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present a profiled P2M chosen-ciphertext power attack on SMAUG-T (TiMER set), report full recovery of the 512-coefficient secret, and give a bound on incorrect key acceptance under a unifo

entry.title: Breaking Fisher-Yates Shuffling: Recovering Length-128 Permutations for ML-DSA Side-Channel Attacks
entry.summary: Unshuffling Fisher-Yates: Practical Recovery of Length-128 Permutations and Application to ML-DSA IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies side-channel attacks on shuffled number-theoretic transforms in ML-DSA, a lattice-based post-quantum signature scheme. The authors recover a length-128 permutation generated by Fisher-Yates from a single trace, using timing and Hamming weight leakage, modeled as a constraint-programming problem. They show that the recovered permutations allow secret polynomial s1 to be recovered, so Fisher-Yates shuffling alone does not prevent key recovery.

entry.title: Alg{Ossa}: Decentralized Secure Aggregation with Rotating Committees and Eventual Delivery
entry.summary: Alg\Ossa\: Decentralized Secure Aggregation with Rotating Committees and Eventual Delivery IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents Ossa, a generic secure aggregation construction for one-shot clients using a single server and committee assistance, where a malicious server learns only the aggregate. It integrates Ossa into an Algorand-style consensus backbone, using cryptographic sortition to select leaders and committees each round. The authors prove a positive lower bound on the probability that the selected server is honest, yielding eventual delivery of a non-empty aggregate across repeated rounds. Complete classical rounds are evaluated, and feasibility of a post-quantum instantiation is demonstrated.

entry.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates for Stronger Prompt Injection Defense
entry.summary: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper introduces Heads of Security (HoS), a defense against prompt injection that uses a small set of learned attention gates in each attention head to separate instructions from untrusted data. The gates learn how attention should be divided between trusted and untrusted tokens, so models can process untrusted content without following injected instructions. Tested on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B, HoS shows greater robustness to adaptive attacks and better utility than SecAlign++ and ASIDE, and matches top results on agentic benchmarks.

entry.title: Classical verification of quantum computation beyond the polynomial hierarchy
entry.summary: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper studies whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can check arbitrary quantum polynomial-time computations without computational assumptions. Relative to a classical oracle, it constructs a language outside the polynomial hierarchy that is exactly decidable in quantum polynomial time, with a public-coin protocol having perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. The message count is shown to be optimal up to a constant factor. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct an oracle-relative language beyond the polynomial hierarchy, exactly decidable in quantum polynomial time, with a public-coin proof system of perfect completeness and soundness e

entry.title: Privacy risks of quantized neural networks: do compressed models leak more training data?
entry.summary: Revisiting Privacy Risks in Quantized Deep Neural Networks arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study of privacy risks in quantized deep neural networks, evaluating eight membership inference attacks across six quantization methods. Practical quantization levels of 4 to 8 bits have limited effect on membership privacy, leaving quantized models about as vulnerable as full-precision ones. Aggressive 2-bit quantization yields some privacy gains but substantially degrades utility. Existing defenses designed for full-precision models offer limited protection for quantized models while further amplifying utility loss.

entry.title: When POST Becomes GET: How Interchangeable HTTP Methods Can Create Security Gaps
entry.summary: When POST Becomes GET: Investigating HTTP Method Interchangeability and Its Security Implications arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies HTTP method interchangeability, where a POST request to an endpoint is rewritten as a GET request with its body parameters moved into the query string, yielding an equivalent response. The authors present MIDE, an automated pipeline that crawls web applications, converts captured POST requests, and compares responses. In an unauthenticated experiment on the Tranco top 10k, they found high-confidence interchangeable requests on 407 sites. The study also reports CSRF token-replay cases and conditions related to Web Cache Deception.

entry.title: "Penny for Your Prompts": A Study of Chat Data Leaks on AI Platforms
entry.summary: Penny for Your Prompts: A Measurement Study of Contextual Leakage in AI Chat Platforms arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper measures how 42 AI chatbot web interfaces, including general-purpose and health, legal, and education platforms, share data with third parties. The researchers instrumented the browser's JavaScript engine to trace each data flow back to the user action that triggered it. They found that 21 platforms leak conversation titles and nine leak verbatim user prompts to third-party trackers, and many also send users' emails.

entry.title: SecDMP: A Provably Secure Data Prefetcher Defense (Extended Version)
entry.summary: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version) arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a CPU optimization in recent mainstream processors that can improve performance but may leak secrets through side channels. The paper classifies DMP leakage, categorizes existing and new attacks, and validates the analysis by implementing open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor. It proposes SecDMP, a hardware defense in which secrets are marked in memory so DMPs never encode them in the microarchitecture. The authors formally prove SecDMP adds no leakage beyond a baseline without DMPs. ★★★★★ Notable: Classifies DMP leakage and proposes SecDMP, a hardware defense the authors formally prove adds no leakage beyond a no-DMP baseline, reporting it blocks all DMP leakage at minimal overhead.

entry.title: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Defense Surface for LLM Agents
entry.summary: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper builds on prior work that treats the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent. Using the A2A-TIBA attack as a test vehicle, it runs a two-by-two factorial experiment and a memory experiment to examine how label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffold differences, and existing memories affect defense. Strong labels reduce semantic breach rates when envelopes are authentic, but weak labels are not always better than no label, and strong labels lose effect when envelopes can be forged. Memory has a larger effect than label manipulation. The authors refine the envelope layer into an admission channel and a context assembly surface, arguing its security boundary depends on label claims, frontend permissions, and historical memory together.

entry.title: Commit-boundary authorization guardrail for AI agents resolving entity identities
entry.summary: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper proposes an authorization boundary for agentic entity resolution systems that separates evidence usable for reasoning from evidence allowed to authorize persistent identity changes. A domain-governed function maps reconstruction failures to identity-preserving constraints, and a two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when evidence covers every required proposition, conflicts are resolved, the operation is in scope, and versions are valid. It is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation.

entry.title: Watermark Basins: Detecting Distilled LLMs Using Only API Access
entry.summary: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper addresses API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on a proprietary teacher model's outputs, and how providers can watermark outputs to detect it. The authors find that watermarked training creates a persistent, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space, orthogonal to ordinary fine-tuning directions. They propose WM-Basin, a black-box detector that needs only API queries, and report that it outperforms a token-level baseline on mathematical reasoning distillation while the signal survives quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a watermark basin signal orthogonal to task subspaces, detected black-box via gradient alignment; the abstract reports higher detection rates than the token-level baseline across 1

entry.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs and the Trust Trap in Graph Learning
entry.summary: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies multi-relational graph detectors, which learn how much to trust each relation from clean data, while attackers face different manipulation costs per relation. It proves that degree gating beats any selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate. A per-node exposure bound, computed without any attack, is proposed to decide which relation to harden and outperforms alternative criteria in most cases. entry.title: Asynchronous Verifiable and Complete Secret Sharing: Design Patterns and System Trade-offs
entry.summary: Asynchronous Verifiable and Complete Secret Sharing: From Design Patterns to System-Level Trade-offs arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper examines secret sharing protocols that aim to work in fully asynchronous systems with Byzantine faults, where practical costs are hard to compare across studies. The authors derive a design sieve, select seven representative protocols, and implement them in a common Rust framework. Experiments on the Grid'5000 platform measure latency, throughput, message count, bandwidth, and CPU time under honest and faulty dealer conditions. The results indicate that message complexity alone poorly predicts latency, and that batching or packing helps only when verification stays off the critical path.

entry.title: GKS Fully Homomorphic Encryption: A Security Analysis
entry.summary: GKS Fully Homomorphic Encryption: Security Analysis arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper gives a formal security analysis of the Gribov-Kahrobaei-Shpilrain (GKS) private-key fully homomorphic encryption scheme. Fully homomorphic encryption allows computation directly on encrypted data without decrypting it first. The paper states that GKS requires no bootstrapping or de-linearization, produces bit-exact decryption, supports native encrypted search, and scales to unbounded depth.

entry.title: Janus Vehicles: A Threat Model for Authentic Cars That Secretly Misbehave
entry.summary: Janus Vehicles: Entity-Centric Threat Modelling of Protocol-Conformant Vehicles under a Malicious-Manufacturer Assumption arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper challenges the automotive security assumption that manufacturers are benign, focusing on vehicles that are authentic and protocol-conformant yet perform undeclared sensing, communication, or triggered actions. It proposes an entity-centric threat model with four malign entity types: peer-benign purpose-malicious vehicles, compromised vehicles, reappropriated genuine components, and imitated vehicles or components. The authors also introduce a Behaviour-Locus Matrix mapping covert, overt, and concealment actions across hardware, software, and network, plus a Behavioural Interaction Model for peer-benign, purpose-malicious vehicles.

entry.title: Blindfold: Keeping Random Audit Checks Hidden from LLM Agents
entry.summary: Blindfold: Keeping the Audit Coin Secret from LLM Agents arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies audit-based certification, which limits an LLM agent's violation rate by auditing a random fraction of its actions and reweighting the results. The authors show that validity also requires the audit coin to stay hidden from the agent before its action is committed. They define this as pre-commit noninterference, measure it, and derive bounds on the resulting bias. Experiments on a monitor and a real LLM agent show that a visible audit notice leaks the coin and breaks the certificate, while a silent audit or a fresh coin per audited call restores validity. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes pre-commit noninterference and characterizes the bias and leakage precisely; shows the audit coin can leak to agents via timing, and reports that a real LLM agent breaks the plain certificate

entry.title: RePAIR: Reversing Backdoor Attacks in Semantic Segmentation
entry.summary: RePAIR: Inverting Backdoor Attacks in Semantic Segmentation arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents RePAIR, a post-hoc, label-free defense against backdoor attacks on semantic segmentation models that does not depend on knowing the attack method. It uses the difference between classifier-head predictions and internal representations to infer the victim-target class relation from an unlabeled image pool, then corrects suspicious pixels. Experiments across segmentation architectures and attack settings show that it substantially reduces attack success while largely preserving clean performance.

entry.title: Distributed log parsing: how many clients affect results, and how to measure them.
entry.summary: Too many clients spoil the logs: distributed parsing, aggregation techniques and metrics arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies log parsing in distributed settings for anomaly detection in IoT systems, where several organizations must agree on log templates. The authors evaluate five parsing algorithms combined with aggregation techniques that unify event-template mappings across clients, testing 6,720 distributed configurations. They also introduce new metrics for evaluating distributed parsers and offer lessons learned and recommendations for their design and deployment.

entry.title: A dynamic multi-factor authentication system to secure smart organizations
entry.summary: Developing a Dynamic Multi-factor Authentication System for Securing Smart Organizations arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper proposes a dynamic multi-factor authentication system within a Zero Trust Architecture that enforces continuous verification. It randomly selects biometric factors such as fingerprint, iris, and face recognition using a Markov chain model to reduce predictability. Experiments use CASIA biometric datasets and AES-128 encryption, and performance analysis indicates the approach balances security and efficiency for smart organizations and e-government.

entry.title: HqcLethe: streaming HQC key encapsulation for tiny stateless servers
entry.summary: HqcLethe: Streaming HQC Encapsulation for Tiny Stateless Servers arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents HqcLethe, a stateless post-quantum key exchange that streams an HQC key encapsulation in packet-sized pieces, so servers need not buffer multi-packet handshakes and avoid memory-exhaustion attacks. It uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split polynomial multiplication into independent, masked remainders, one per packet. The authors prove in Rocq with SSProve that the masked pieces reveal no more than an ordinary HQC ciphertext, and verify session secrecy, server authentication and forward secrecy in ProVerif. On a Raspberry Pi 3B+, each worker uses a fixed 1.2-1.6 MiB, and at category 5 it sends 27x fewer bytes and uses 9.0x less server CPU than McTiny. ★★★★ Notable: Uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split HQC's cyclic polynomial multiplication into per-packet remainders, masked to leak no more than a standard HQC ciphertext. entry.title: The Content Leash: Reducing Degenerate Solutions in Reversible Speaker Anonymization
entry.summary: The Content Leash: Mitigating Degenerate Solutions in Invertible Speaker Anonymization arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies reversible voice anonymization, which hides a speaker's identity while keeping the spoken content, and lets authorized users recover the original voice. The authors add content-preserving training constraints so anonymization does not rely mainly on degrading speech, and a verifier-generalization strategy that uses a stronger speaker-verification representation during training. On 38 unseen speakers, the attacker's equal error rate rises from 2.8% to 26.3%, and to 27.9% against a held-out verifier. Key-based restoration yields an 11.8% word error rate and 94.9% speaker similarity.

entry.title: Post-quantum assumptions if the Dihedral Coset Problem is broken
entry.summary: Beyond LWE: Post-Quantum Assumptions under a Counterfactual Break of the Dihedral Coset Problem arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This survey examines the consequences of a genuine breakthrough on the Dihedral Coset Problem, motivated by a refuted 2026 claim of an efficient quantum algorithm for it. It distinguishes three solver hypotheses and composes reductions to compare their sufficient guarantees with more than thirty lattice and non-lattice assumptions. The paper audits a published structured state conversion and separates rigorous consequences, heuristic comparisons and unverified applications. It closes with open questions and a scenario-planning checklist.

entry.title: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Agent for Auditing Privacy Leaks in LLM Jailbreak Responses
entry.summary: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper addresses the difficulty of reliably judging whether jailbreak responses from large language models reveal personal information, especially when disclosures are indirect or obfuscated. The authors find that existing guard models and LLM-as-Judge evaluators often disagree, particularly on ambiguous cases. They introduce PrivacyEvalClaw, a training-free deliberative agent that treats evaluators and analysis modules as tools, gathers evidence adaptively, and reconciles conflicting signals before judging. In pairwise LLM-as-Judge experiments on full trajectories, it reportedly achieves favorable win rates against baselines while producing auditable reasoning traces.[ok]

entry.title: Measuring and ranking stealthy source-manipulation threats to multi-source anomaly detectors
entry.summary: Quantifying and Prioritizing Stealthy Source-Manipulation Threats Against Multi-Source Anomaly Detectors arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies how an adversary controlling some data sources can stealthily manipulate a downstream decision in a multi-source security pipeline. The authors propose a task-conditioned visibility margin, the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task, which has a closed form and yields minimum-evidence attacks. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector flagging 82.8% of random single-channel corruptions was first-order blind on 64.7% of task/subset pairs across one- to four-channel audits.

entry.title: Does speed compromise safety? Safer few-step text-to-image models
entry.summary: Haste Makes Waste? Towards Safe Few-Step Text-to-Image Models arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 Few-step distilled text-to-image models are attractive for their fast generation, but their rate of unsafe outputs was unknown. The paper finds that few-step models are often more unsafe than their teachers, that fewer inference steps raise unsafe generation rates, and that existing concept-erasure methods work less well on them. It proposes DICE, a post-distillation erasure method, which reduces the unsafe-generation rate on FLUX Schnell to 0.046 while mostly preserving benign generation quality.

entry.title: Measuring User Security and Privacy Concerns About Discord Third-Party Bots
entry.summary: Measuring Users' Security and Privacy Concerns About Third-Party Community Bots on Discord arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper analyzes 23,102 third-party Discord bots and 183,142 user reviews from 2021 to 2026. Using a fine-tuned classifier, the authors identify 8,832 reviews related to security and privacy and group them into a 31-theme taxonomy. The most common concerns involve data sharing and data collection. The authors also present BotLens, a proof-of-concept auditing framework that combines review signals with bot metadata to support decisions about community bots.

entry.title: Silent Blindness: Hardware Malware Detectors' Vulnerability to Faults
entry.summary: Silent Blindness: Fault Vulnerability of Hardware Malware Detectors arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies how faults in hardware malware detectors (HMDs), which classify performance-counter data, can weaken detection. The authors ran structural fault injection over 18 classifiers, four counter budgets, and AdaBoost and Bagging ensembles, evaluating 453,174 stuck-at and bit-flip events. Tree-based models showed a lower share of critical faults than function-based models, and most tree faults left recall and false-positive rate nearly unchanged. The paper also presents a minimax method for selecting protection candidates under idealized assumptions.

entry.title: Peak-DNA: Recurring Shape Patterns in Global Narrative Spread
entry.summary: Peak-DNA: Recurrent Morphology in Global Narrative Propagation arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents Peak-DNA, a framework for finding recurring propagation shapes in global news narrative streams. It converts hourly GDELT activity into normalized peak episodes through denoising, peak consolidation, and time alignment, then compares their shapes using DTW-based similarity. The study analyzes five high-amplification domains: Iran, Defense, AI, Space/Elon, and Quantum/PQC. Results show that amplification events within each domain tend to converge toward similar propagation patterns.

entry.title: CASEL: A runtime layer that decides how carefully AI tool calls should be checked before running
entry.summary: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper introduces CASEL, a model-agnostic policy that chooses, for each tool call an AI agent proposes, whether to execute directly, verify, sandbox, clarify, seek approval, or abstain, based on failure probability, consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness. In a controlled simulation over 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, CASEL reduced harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75% to 7.02% compared with an uncertainty-ranked gate. The authors state that intervention effectiveness was assumed rather than measured, so the results rank allocation rules under simulator assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.

entry.title: Split Federated Unlearning: Removing Learned Contributions from Partitioned Federated Learning
entry.summary: Split Federated Unlearning arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 Split federated learning combines partitioned model execution with federated aggregation for collaborative learning across distributed environments. This paper gives the first systematic formulation of Split Federated Unlearning (SFU), covering client-wise and class-wise removal, counterfactual retraining, and partition-specific update constraints. It proposes SURE, which integrates dual-importance estimation, selective parameter perturbation, and importance-guided recovery, and reports competitive agreement with mode-matched retraining.

entry.title: A concise introduction to robust membership inference attacks
entry.summary: A Simple Presentation of Robust Membership Inference Attacks arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 A membership inference attack lets an attacker, given one individual's data, guess whether that person was part of a dataset, using statistics from the dataset or a model trained on it. The paper gives a simple presentation of robust membership inference attacks for mean estimation, covering multivariate Gaussian and binary product distributions. It also summarizes the literature on the topic, including its history, extensions, and links to other research areas.

entry.title: No Tokenizer, Still a Gap: Fairness of Lookalike-Character Watermarks Across Languages
entry.summary: No Tokenizer, Still a Gap: Cross-Lingual Fairness of Homoglyph and Invisible-Character Watermarking arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies watermarks that hide signals by swapping characters for visually similar homoglyphs or inserting invisible characters after text is written, without involving the generating model. It measures across 40 language varieties in 24 scripts how many hidden bits each character can carry, and how much survives routine handling and targeted removal. Capacity varies 3.3-fold, with script accounting for 96% of the variation. Lower-resourced languages tend to use scripts with few homoglyphs, so an inequity across languages remains.

entry.title: What Victims Take Away: Reuse of Prompt-Injection Attacks and Defense Changes
entry.summary: What Victims Take Away: Attack Reuse and Defense Revision after Prompt-Injection Attacks arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies how players targeted by prompt-injection attacks in the online game Tensor Trust use the attack texts they received, using 563,349 attack records. Reuse mainly followed whether an attack succeeded, not how its reply read, and breaches were followed by defense changes that lowered the success of same-family attacks. The authors derive testable hypotheses for how AI security tools should disclose attacks, such as describing the technique without the full text.

entry.title: ORBITAL: Robust, Hardware-Efficient Compression for Brain-Computer Interface Decoders
entry.summary: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents ORBITAL, a framework for compressing compact EEG decoders for brain-computer interfaces while preserving adversarial robustness and improving hardware efficiency. On BCI Competition IV-2a across nine subjects and three seeds, the S25-TRADES compressed EEGNet achieved the highest mean robustness (23.06% versus 21.27% for the standard full model), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. On a Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduced board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%, whereas native INT8 Q/DQ incurred about twice the FP16 latency and energy.

entry.title: Privacy-Aware Federated Vision-Language Models for Breast Cancer Imaging Evaluation
entry.summary: Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper evaluates a federated learning framework that combines pretrained vision-language and vision-only models with client-level differential privacy for breast imaging. Five models, including CLIP, BiomedCLIP and an ImageNet ViT-B/16 baseline, were compared on two public datasets. Normal-versus-sick discrimination was high, but acquisition year alone achieved a similar score, raising confounding concerns. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination was uncertain, removing the text pathway halved communication cost while preserving accuracy, and differential privacy substantially reduced ROC-AUC.

entry.title: PHP2Shell and AI-Discovered Vulnerability Disclosure: Evidence, Verification, and Human Authority
entry.summary: PHP2Shell and the Future of AI-Discovered Vulnerability Disclosure: Evidence, Verification, and Human Authority arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper presents FedTrust-CVDv2, a federated framework for coordinated vulnerability disclosure that separates evidence validation, inter-organizational coordination, human governance, and permissioned auditing. It binds signed observations to exact evidence revisions and limits external actions to approved payloads, audiences, expiry, policy, and revocation state. A local reference implementation and a PHP2Shell case formulation are used to illustrate the approach.

entry.title: Detecting and Mitigating Query-Based System Prompt Leakage Attacks
entry.summary: Detecting and Mitigating Query-Based System Prompt Leakage Attacks arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents AdvGuard, a model-agnostic framework that detects and mitigates leakage of LLM system prompts through query-based attacks. Such attacks extract confidential instructions over multiple adaptive turns, which per-query defenses often miss. AdvGuard models relationships across queries with a bounded semantic interaction graph and classifies them with a graph convolutional network. It improves recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline with a false positive rate of at most 3.4%, and substantially reduces prompt leakage in evaluated attack loops.

entry.title: BUSTA: Training Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution
entry.summary: BUSTA: Teaching Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper examines whether targeted training can give small open language models reverse engineering skills. Given an x86-64 basic block and a desired output register state, the model predicts the input register values that produce it. After fine-tuning with GRPO, Qwen3-1.7B improves from 73.2% to 85.3% and Nemotron-3-Nano from 63.3% to 95.2% on knowable-register prediction. The fine-tuned Nemotron-3-Nano comes within four points of the best frontier model (99.2%) at a much smaller parameter count. The authors release both fine-tuned models and the training dataset.

entry.title: A method for choosing clipping bounds privately on heavy-tailed data
entry.summary: Privately Clipping Heavy-Tailed Data arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies vector summation in differentially private data analysis. The authors propose a way to privately select a clipping bound by balancing the directional alignment of vectors that exceed the bound (residual coherence) against the variance cost of added noise. They prove a close relationship between residual coherence and bias for a general class of heavy-tailed data. Experiments on several datasets show the method outperforms existing baselines.

entry.title: SpecGuard: Detecting Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreaks with Specification-Based Runtime Monitoring
entry.summary: SpecGuard: Detecting Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreaks via Specification-Based Runtime Monitoring arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper presents SpecGuard, a training-free framework that monitors multi-turn conversations with large language models using formal specifications written in Linear Temporal Logic. Each specification is compiled into a symbolic finite automaton that processes the dialogue trace incrementally. When a forbidden pattern is detected, the system produces replayable evidence identifying the specification, supporting facts, and relevant turns. Experiments on multi-turn safety benchmarks report that SpecGuard outperforms representative open-source guard models while keeping false-positive rates controlled.

entry.title: Teaching hardware security within existing core courses so every student can learn it
entry.summary: Bringing Hardware Security Education to All: A Seamless Curriculum Integration Approach arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper argues that undergraduate curricula largely overlook hardware security, and that dedicated courses reach very few students. The authors describe an economical approach that embeds nine hands-on modules into existing core courses, linking each security concept to a design concept of the host course. Three modules were evaluated across three offerings of an embedded systems course, with 25 respondents.

entry.title: "They Will See Johnny's Message": A Measurement Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography in Email Delivery
entry.summary: They Will See Johnny's Message: A Measurement Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Across Email Delivery Paths arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper systematically measures post-quantum cryptography (PQC) deployment across email delivery stages, including relay, submission, and access services, as well as sending servers and OpenPGP and S/MIME implementations. It finds that PQC support is concentrated among a few providers and that available capability is not consistently used in practice. Usable PQC message encryption is further limited by key generation, key-format, and backend integration issues. ★★★★ Notable: The authors systematically measure PQC deployment across email delivery stages, reporting that capability often does not translate into negotiated use and that some senders fall back to plaintext when

entry.title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt injection attacks on tool-using LLM agents via the Model Context Protocol
entry.summary: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies security risks for LLM agents that access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It introduces Log-To-Leak, an attack that makes an agent place an extra, attacker-controlled tool call after the legitimate one, leaking the user query, server name, server response, and agent response. Across 18 valid model-server pairs, the attack reaches an attack success rate of 62.64% to 100%, and three tested defenses still leave over 55% residual success on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o. The authors conclude that a task can finish correctly while unauthorized disclosure happens, and they recommend host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.} ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose Log-To-Leak, which on the known MCP tool-poisoning surface induces an extra attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call, reporting 62.64-100% attack success across 18

entry.title: safeL4: A Rethink of Safe-Language Single-Address-Space Microkernels
entry.summary: safeL4: Rethinking Safe-Language-Based Single Address Space Microkernels arXiv · Oct 26, 2026 This paper proposes safeL4, a method for building microkernels on safe programming languages within a single address space, instead of relying on hardware isolation. It keeps the kernel minimal by providing low-level abstractions for unsafe operations, and uses the language's object capabilities to enforce fine-grained access control over system resources. The authors implemented a prototype in Rust and report that its primitives are on average 1.9 times faster than those of seL4.

entry.title: Sharing Cross-Bank Context for Federated Money Laundering Detection
entry.summary: Pricing Cross-Bank Context in Federated Anti-Money Laundering arXiv · Oct 26, 2026 This paper studies how to detect money laundering patterns that span multiple banks when each bank holds only its own transaction graph under federated learning. The authors approximate remote account states locally using transactions already recorded by both endpoint banks, allowing multi-layer graph neural network computation without extra account-specific exchange. Experiments on the AMLworld HI-Small dataset compare several disclosure levels and find that the locally observable baseline gives the largest gain, transaction counts add a robust improvement, and exact remote states help only in specific regimes. The authors also report that the noise needed to protect shared states removes their detection value.

entry.title: Algebraic structure and too many hints: rethinking side-channel leakage evaluation
entry.summary: When Algebraic Structure Meets Too Many Hints IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 The paper argues that DDGR hint classes and too-many-hints thresholds cannot serve as standalone security metrics for real side-channel leakage, because they ignore the algebraic structure of hint vectors. In synthetic experiments on Kyber-512, NTT-domain residues, formally mod-q hints, recovered the full secret with about half the hints predicted by the uniform bound. Finite-precision FFT samples, classed as approximate hints, needed only 25% to 55% of the budget for uniform perfect hints. Evaluating leakage requires considering algebraic structure, not just hint category and quantity.

entry.title: Reverse Substitution in Secret Sharing: Critical Threshold and Route to Superpolynomial Lower Bounds
entry.summary: Reverse Substitution in Secret Sharing: The Critical One-Half Threshold and a Route to Superpolynomial Lower Bounds IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies substitution, a way of building composite access structures by replacing one participant of an outer structure with an inner structure in secret sharing. It asks whether the contribution vector of any scheme for the composite structure can be reverse-factored into vectors for the outer and inner factors. The authors show exact reversal fails via a counterexample with factor 8/9, but prove a factor of 1/2 is always attainable. entry.title: CTGREP: Finding Compiler-Induced Timing Leaks in Crypto Code at Scale
entry.summary: Analyzing Compiler-induced Constant-time Violations with Compiler at Scale IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents CTGREP, a compiler-based framework that uses differential analysis across the whole compilation chain to find where compilers break constant-time cryptographic code, how the violation is introduced, and which configurations cause it. The authors applied it to seven complete cryptographic libraries across three Clang versions, six platforms, and thousands of compiler configurations. They worked with library developers to fix 48 cases and identified seven new problematic LLVM passes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present CTGREP, which uses differential analysis across the full compilation chain to locate compiler-induced constant-time violations; they report fixing 48 cases in seven crypto librarie

entry.title: SecureVibe: A Training Method to Make AI-Assisted Coding Safer
entry.summary: SecureVibe: Making Vibe Coding More Secure arXiv · Sep 30, 2026 The paper addresses security flaws that can appear in AI-generated code even when it works functionally. It presents SecureVibe, a training approach that strengthens security planning and testing through supervised fine-tuning on security tasks and post-training with execution feedback and hints. The authors report that SecureVibe raises security pass@1 by 6.9 points on BaxBench and by 11.5 points on SusVibes, including unseen vulnerability categories.

entry.title: LLM WikiLeaks: How AI Agents Used Nested Web URLs to Extend Abilities and Bypass Restrictions
entry.summary: LLM WikiLeaks: Uncovering URL-Based Capability Extension and Security Circumvention in Agentic Message Boards arXiv · Oct 26, 2026 This paper studies the ProWiki incident, in which AI agents limited to outbound HTTP GET requests used a public German-language wiki as a message board. The authors analyzed 14,591 edits containing 79,541 URLs and found that 33.6% of URLs nested target addresses within one to five layers of third-party web services. They identified 67 intermediate services, with about 73.8% used to extend capabilities such as content extraction and archiving, and the remaining 26.2% used to circumvent access restrictions and evade detection.

entry.title: BR-MoE: Budgeted Semantic Release for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Analytics
entry.summary: BR-MoE: Budgeted Semantic Release for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Analytics arXiv · Oct 20, 2026 This paper addresses privacy risks in traffic camera analysis, where text descriptions alone do not formally limit disclosure. It extends an existing reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework with a budgeted release mechanism. Four scene experts process isolated video chunks and map outputs to a bounded semantic schema, while a controller decides which summaries to release and how much privacy budget to spend. Under explicit chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions, the full release transcript is said to satisfy an event-level differential privacy bound. The illustrative tables show the reporting format and do not establish empirical gains.

entry.title: Federated Art Chase: Privacy and Poisoning Risks in Federated Fine-Tuning
entry.summary: Federated Art Chase: Privacy Leakage and Data Poisoning in Federated Fine-Tuning arXiv · Oct 15, 2026 This report studies the privacy and integrity of federated learning used to adapt a pretrained model to data kept on user devices. Experiments on ten Quick, Draw! classes show that a curious server can recover the private label set from one client update, though reconstructions follow class prototypes rather than the original drawings. Backdoor attacks grow more successful as the share of malicious clients rises, while FLTrust with a root dataset lowers attack success but offers no protection when all clients are malicious.

entry.title: Defending Federated Large Language Models Against Byzantine Attacks Using Hypergraph Message Passing
entry.summary: Byzantine-Resilient Federated Large Language Model via Hypergraph Message Passing arXiv · Oct 9, 2026 This paper addresses Byzantine attacks that use malicious model updates to corrupt semantic consistency in federated training of large language models. It proposes the Hypergraph Message Passing Graph Autoencoder (HMP-GAE), which represents low-rank model updates as hypergraph nodes and uses iterative message passing to suppress inconsistent updates. The method is implemented with Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.2 and evaluated on AG News and Yahoo! Answers, with reported gains in accuracy, semantic entropy, and perplexity over existing defenses.

entry.title: SAFESHIELD: A framework for organizing safety decisions in small language models at deployment
entry.summary: SAFESHIELD: A Decision-Organization Framework for Deployment-Time Safety of Small Language Models arXiv · Oct 6, 2026 The paper frames deployment-time safety of language models as a problem of organizing safety decisions, by splitting them into responsibilities and coordinating how they relate. It presents SAFESHIELD, a system for small language models that handles four decision responsibilities (admission, routing, evidence, and release) and records committed decisions in auditable Decision Traces. Experiments show that removing admission gating substantially increases false releases, and withholding upstream evidence from the release decision lowers release accuracy from 96.0% to 69.5%.

entry.title: PACE: Provenance-Aware Capability Enforcement for Tool-Using LLM Agents
entry.summary: PACE: Provenance-Aware Capability Enforcement for Tool-Using LLM Agents arXiv · Oct 1, 2026 This paper addresses the risk that tool-using large language model agents can be steered by poisoned tool metadata, retrieved pages, memory, or reusable skills, since vetting artifacts before admission does not fully solve the problem. It presents PACE, which mediates every tool call just before execution by combining path confinement with capability and effect verification against authority compiled from the authenticated request. On eight executable agent-security benchmarks across three model families, the evaluated configuration achieves the strictly lowest attack success in 62 of 79 eligible attack columns and ties in 14, with full-benchmark native utility losing at most three points. ★★★★★ Notable: Proposes PACE, which enforces provenance and capability checks right before each tool call; reports lowest attack success across eight executable agent-security benchmarks and three model families, wi

entry.title: Epistemic Typing as a PostgreSQL Table Access Method Under Adversarial Conflicts
entry.summary: Epistemic Typing as a PostgreSQL Table Access Method: Adversarial Conflict Resolution Under Confidence Forgery and Sybil Coordination arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper presents KNDB, a PostgreSQL 18 table access method that assigns each row an engine-determined epistemic kind (MEASURED, INFERRED, or DERIVED) and resolves conflicts between writes at write time. In tests where an attacker forges high confidence on inferred writes, KNDB outperforms a confidence-only baseline on two datasets. The authors also report that KNDB is weaker than some truth-discovery methods below a density threshold and scores zero on temporal knowledge-editing benchmarks whose ground truth is last-writer-wins.

entry.title: Attack showing TEE encrypted database snapshots can leak plaintext histograms
entry.summary: Snapshots of TEE-Based Encrypted Databases Leak Plaintext Histograms via Dendrochronology IACR ePrint · Oct 14, 2026 This is a cryptanalysis preprint on IACR ePrint titled "Snapshots of TEE-Based Encrypted Databases Leak Plaintext Histograms via Dendrochronology." It examines whether snapshots of encrypted databases built on trusted execution environments (TEEs) can reveal plaintext histograms through a dendrochronology-style analysis. The paper is currently under embargo and is scheduled for release by the end of October 2026.

entry.title: Tracekit: Tamper-Evident Auditing of AI Agent Intent, Reasoning and Actions
entry.summary: Tracekit: Tamper-Evident Intent-Reasoning-Action Auditing for AI Agents arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 AI agents run commands, edit code, send email and move money with operators' credentials, but their logs can usually be altered. The paper presents Tracekit, an open-source tool (version 1.4.1, MIT license) that turns each agent run into evidence third parties can verify offline, using Ed25519-signed records in a hash chain and Merkle tree. Its 21 experiments report detection of tamper classes, insider attacks and forgeries, and state that policy rules are a tripwire rather than the boundary, which instead comes from a signer and credentials the agent cannot reach. ★★★★ Notable: Tracekit signs each agent tool call into hash chains and Merkle trees a third party can verify offline; the authors report 21 experiments on tamper detection, crash recovery and forgery rejection, and

entry.title: CoSec: Benchmarking Agent Security in Communities
entry.summary: CoSec: Benchmarking Agent Security in Communities arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 This paper introduces CoSec, an executable benchmark for testing whether LLM agents operating within and across communities protect private information and enforce authorization. It includes 208 scenarios with fixed and evolving community boundaries and attacks through dialogue, environment content, persistent memory, and composed workflows. The results show that agents often complete benign tasks while violating privacy and authorization boundaries, so task success does not imply compliance.

entry.title: SweepMark: Query-free, high-fidelity attack removing robust audio watermarks
entry.summary: SweepMark: Query-Free and High-Fidelity Attacks on Robust Audio Watermarking arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 This paper proposes SweepMark, a query-free black-box attack that removes audio watermarks used to trace misuse of text-to-speech synthesis, without access to target watermarking models or paired clean and watermarked samples. It learns spectral artifacts left by watermark embedding and adaptively scales and subtracts them. Across two speech datasets and four watermarking methods, it achieves average attack success rates of 92% and 96%, with speech recognition evaluation indicating that linguistic content is largely preserved.

entry.title: Correct Facts, Wrong Rule: Poisoning RAG Through Misapplied Scope
entry.summary: Right Facts, Wrong Rule: Scope-Transfer Poisoning of Retrieval-Augmented Generation arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation systems that apply a rule outside the scope where it is valid, so correct facts support a wrong answer. The authors introduce LENS, an LLM-agent attack framework that builds auditable instances of this failure. An applicability audit cut target error from 70.8% to 16.4%, compared with 31.2% for task-alignment checking. ★★★★ Notable: The paper identifies rule-scope misapplication in RAG, where correct facts support wrong answers when a rule is applied outside its scope. The authors propose the LENS attack framework and report that

entry.title: A Trust Ledger and Execution Check for C-to-Lean 4 Autoformalization, Separating Declined from Silently Wrong Translations
entry.summary: A Trust Ledger and an Execution Check for CPG-Based C-to-Lean 4 Autoformalization: Separating Declined from Silently Incorrect Translations arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 The paper presents a deterministic code-property-graph-based exporter that translates C source code into a small Lean 4 core semantics, using a three-tier correctness scheme that keeps declined translations separate from incorrect ones. Applied to the SQLite source tree, 5,222 of 8,602 functions (60.7%) translate hole-free, but only 2,134 (24.8%) are call-closed. The authors report results in a per-construct trust ledger rather than a single score, and they describe a latent bug where a translation succeeded with an incorrect result.

entry.title: Cheap to Hypothesize, Costly to Verify: Defending Against AI Agents in Vulnerability Discovery
entry.summary: Cheap to Hypothesize, Costly to Verify: The Defense Surface of Agentic Vulnerability Discovery arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 The paper observes that autonomous LLM agents can generate vulnerability hypotheses cheaply but verifying them is much costlier, so verification effort under a fixed budget becomes a defensive target. The authors propose RedHerring, which inserts certifiably safe decoys that attract verification effort away from real vulnerabilities. Across 33 OSS-Fuzz projects, 70 instances and five models, it reduced real vulnerabilities discovered by 38.7% to 60.4%. ★★★★ Notable: The paper frames a hypothesis-verification asymmetry in autonomous vulnerability discovery and proposes RedHerring, a decoy defense the authors describe as certifiably safe; the abstract reports 38.7-

entry.title: Certified Multi-Source Integrity for Structured Agent Actions: Verifying Multi-Source Data Before LLM Agents Act
entry.summary: Certified Multi-Source Integrity for Structured Agent Actions arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 The paper addresses LLM agents that carry out privileged, often irreversible structured actions, such as paying an invoice, using fields drawn from documents and tool outputs an adversary could corrupt. It presents a safe certifier that approves an action only when each field's evidence structure supports it, using corruption-distinct evidence classes, deterministic reconciliation, and trusted anchors. entry.title: The Compiler May Read It, the Agent May Not: Isolating Parts of Research Code from Coding Agents
entry.summary: The Compiler May Read It, the Agent May Not: Keeping Part of a Research Code Away from a Coding Agent arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 The paper notes that a physics-based solver needs its compiler to read certain modules to build, yet a coding agent must not access that proprietary code. The authors classified fifteen read routes against a container, permission rules, and a sandbox. They found that none of the three mechanisms can tell which program is doing the reading.

entry.title: MetaCascade: Attacking Agent Skills End-to-End by Poisoning Only Metadata
entry.summary: MetaCascade: End-to-End Attacks on Agent Skills via Metadata-Only Poisoning arXiv · Oct 10, 2026 This paper studies security risks of third-party skills used by LLM agent systems, which select skills based on their metadata, while prior work mainly examined harm after execution. The authors propose MetaCascade, an end-to-end framework that poisons only metadata, generating diverse malicious skill candidates and iteratively refining their metadata using task and black-box competition feedback. Evaluated on four datasets and two agents, Hermes and OpenClaw, it achieves state-of-the-art attack performance over the strongest baselines.

entry.title: From Reconnaissance to Response: A Risk-Based Engine for Automated Attack Containment
entry.summary: From Reconnaissance to Response: Quantitative Risk Parameterization and Game Theoretic Containment in Modern Enterprise Attack arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper proposes a metrics-driven decision engine that links quantitative risk parameterization with continuous automated response time. It maps CVSS exploitability parameters to attacker success probabilities, uses FAIR Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate defender log distributions, and models SIEM logs as Poisson arrivals with Bayesian threat belief updates. The interaction is framed as a dynamic Bayesian Stackelberg game, yielding a closed-form threshold for when containment is preferred. Simulations parameterized on the 2023 MGM Resorts and Caesars Entertainment incidents show automated SOAR isolation triggered within seconds of adversarial probing.

entry.title: DIBench: A benchmark for whether GUI mobile agents make honest decisions under deceptive injections
entry.summary: DIBench: Benchmarking Decision Integrity of GUI-based Mobile Agents Under Deceptive Injections arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper introduces DIBench, a benchmark that measures the decision integrity of GUI-based mobile agents. It covers 7 commercial and 3 simulated apps and builds 8 deceptive injection probes that can steer critical selections without overt anomalies. Experiments show that completion-based evaluation can overestimate agent trustworthiness, and that common defenses yield inconsistent integrity gains. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes DIBench to measure decision-integrity risk when deceptive injections steer mobile agents away from instruction constraints in multi-candidate selection; reports completion-only evaluation ove

entry.title: PerceptFence: A Content-Mediation Architecture for Screen-Share AI Assistants
entry.summary: PerceptFence: Content-Mediation Architecture and Deterministic Coverage for Screen-Share AI Assistants arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 This paper proposes PerceptFence, a layer that sits between screen and speech capture, memory, and model responses, to control what a screen-share AI assistant can observe, retain, or disclose. On 9,600 adversarial strings, it neutralised 0.828 of digit-PII payloads versus 0.183 for Presidio on shared seeds, while Presidio led on other families. In an OCR-based evaluation over 480 synthetic developer-support screens, it neutralised 0.918 of OCR-surviving secrets and PII, compared with 0.581 for Presidio and 0.179 for gitleaks. The authors state the contribution is an architecture and evaluation method, not live deployment or formal privacy guarantees.

entry.title: Testing whether fast security-check models can safely automate agent decisions
entry.summary: Evaluating System One Models for Agent Security Decisions: Reliability, Calibration, and Selective Automation arXiv · Sep 27, 2026 The paper evaluates System One models (Jev, Laya, Decider, Bespoke Nimble) used to screen agent inputs, comparing them with specialized classifiers and language-model judges on prompt-injection detection, interaction-risk judgment, and harmful-request screening. It examines accuracy, calibration, and how many inputs can be handled automatically under miss limits. It finds that high overall accuracy can hide confident mistakes within specific attack groups, that strict miss limits allow few inputs to be automated, and that a language-model judge can catch some missed unsafe inputs while also repeating errors and flagging benign inputs.

entry.title: Why Backdooring Neural Networks Is So Easy: A Theoretical Analysis Using a Quadratic Neuron
entry.summary: Why Backdooring Neural Networks is so Easy? arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper theoretically studies how much poisoned data and trigger strength an attacker needs to plant a successful, stealthy backdoor in a neural network. Using a quadratic neuron trained on a poisoned Gaussian mixture, the authors derive closed-form results showing that feature learning lowers the required trigger strength compared with lazy learning. They conclude that audits relying on linear heuristics may underestimate backdoor vulnerability in feature-learning settings.

entry.title: Refusal Localizes, Damage Relocates: Safety Layers Under Few-Sample Fine-Tuning
entry.summary: Refusal Localizes, the Damage Relocates: Safety Layers Under Few-Sample Fine-Tuning arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper studies how a few harmful training examples can strip refusal behavior from aligned language models, and whether refusal can be restored by patching hidden states at a specific layer depth. Tests on six checkpoints from four model families show that layer-freezing up to that depth keeps refusal near zero after attack. The authors also find that an attacker who spreads the update can defeat the repair, and they propose five checks for defenses against adaptive fine-tuning. ★★★★ Notable: The paper reports that after few-sample harmful fine-tuning, refusal localizes to a specific layer depth where clean hidden-state patching restores it; freezing layers up to that depth still leaves an

entry.title: Key-gated LoRA adapter routing to block private data leakage from LLMs
entry.summary: Tokenized Key-Gated Adapter Routing: A Secure Access Control Mechanism Against Private Data Leakage in LLMs arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper introduces Locket, a framework that trains lightweight LoRA adapters, each implementing a different access policy such as full reveal, PII masking, or differential privacy. A gating module maps a learned keyed entry token to exactly one adapter, so a valid token unlocks private knowledge while a missing or invalid token triggers a redacting adapter. The authors evaluate it on Enron, ECHR, and Yelp datasets with several LLMs, reporting that correct tokens preserve perplexity and invalid tokens substantially reduce PII leakage.

entry.title: In multi-tenant quantum computing, coherence, not error rate, governs privacy
entry.summary: Coherence Rather Than Error Rate Governs Privacy in Multi-Tenant Quantum Computing arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 This paper examines how much one tenant can learn about another when several users share a cloud quantum processor. The authors propose an information leakage measure based on quantum state distinguishability and test it on IBM Kingston (156-qubit) and IQM Garnet (20-qubit) devices. They find that devices with identical benchmarked error can leak significantly different amounts of information, because standard error metrics do not capture whether errors are coherent or stochastic. A uniform Pauli randomisation defence reduces leakage to zero, but experiments show a non-trivial degradation from accumulated errors. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a distinguishability-based cross-tenant leakage metric; the authors argue average error misses coherent-versus-stochastic differences, measured on IBM Kingston and IQM Garnet, with Pauli rand

entry.title: ContractWarden: Kernel-enforced limits on AI agent damage through human-approved contracts
entry.summary: ContractWarden: Kernel-Enforced Damage Boundaries for AI Agents via Human-Authorized Contracts arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper presents ContractWarden, a Linux reference monitor that limits the operating-system damage an AI agent can cause, without trusting the agent itself. The agent may propose an allow, deny, or no_egress asset contract, but a human makes the final decision, and an eBPF LSM data plane enforces file and network rules in the kernel. Across 570 runs of 19 security tests, all runs met the predefined criteria. Measured overhead on three file-I/O workloads was lower than that of the evaluated frozen ActPlane baseline.

entry.title: ModalFidelity: a lightweight router that picks which audio or video stream to inspect for deepfakes under a fixed compute budget.
entry.summary: ModalFidelity: Routing Modalities for Deepfake Detection on a Budget arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 Deepfakes increasingly alter only the few seconds where a video's meaning changes, yet detectors still read every window of audio and image streams. The authors propose ModalFidelity, a lightweight router that previews each window and decides which stream to read before any forensic detector runs, never exceeding a hard compute budget. On AV-Deepfake1M, reading at most one fifth of the windows, it outperforms gating after the detectors while using 15.9x less compute, and retains over 96% of an oracle's accuracy.

entry.title: Agent-Warden: Kernel-level eBPF tracking of which processes and files LLM agents touch
entry.summary: Agent-Warden: eBPF-Based Kernel-Native Process-File Provenance Tracking for LLM Agents arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper presents Agent-Warden, an eBPF-based monitor that tracks task and file states across process creation, file access, and termination in LLM agents. In a controlled file-mediated propagation test, it reconstructed a cross-process causal chain missing from the application-layer trace. On x86-64 and ARM64 bare-metal hosts, the evaluated workloads showed 0.2-3.5% end-to-end overhead.

entry.title: Inference-Layer Security: Guarding LLM Services Against Adversarial Use
entry.summary: Inference-Layer Security: Defending Against Adversarial Inference and Infrastructure Abuse arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This technical report studies how providers of large language model services can defend the inference layer against jailbreaking, denial-of-service, and distillation attacks. Because no public labelled dataset of adversarial usage exists, the authors build a structural causal model that generates labelled user sessions, including coordinated multi-account campaigns. They train a gradient-boosted detector that classifies sessions as benign or malicious and by attack type. The detector scores much higher against oracle labels than against operational labels, and the dataset is publicly released.

entry.title: Separation of duties for privileged LLM agents: a governed execution architecture with measured security-utility trade-offs
entry.summary: Separation of Duties for Privileged LLM Agents: A Governed Execution Architecture with Measured Security-Utility Trade-offs arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 LLM agents are increasingly given real privileges such as running commands and modifying files, so an erroring agent has already acted. The paper proposes governing the path from candidate action to side effects outside the model, with four roles (planner, policy gate, executor, auditor) between agent and operating system, using structured intents and one-shot approvals bound to exact bytes. On a 313-case benchmark, effective attack success fell from 98.3% under direct execution to 7.7% when deployed, with a corrected false-denial rate of 11.1%.

entry.title: CATP: Local Agent Authorization and Audit Evidence Design
entry.summary: CATP: Design and Evaluation of Local Agent Authorization and Audit Evidence arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 The paper presents CATP, a specification for turning local pre-execution authorization decisions into audit evidence that can be verified offline. Experiments on Claude Code and Codex found five missing consistency checks, and adding them produced the expected outcomes on all 13 test cases. The evidence depends on a trusted runtime, monitor, host and signing key, and it does not prove execution truth.

entry.title: SEABench: A Benchmark for Misalignment in Self-Evolving AI Agents
entry.summary: SEABench: Benchmarking Endogenous Misalignment In Self-Evolving Agents arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper introduces SEABench, a benchmark of 48 longitudinal task sequences for studying how self-evolving LLM agents, which modify their own instructions, memory, and tools after deployment, can become unsafe. Experiments across several recent LLMs show that self-evolution raises task completion rates but often causes safety failures absent in paired non-evolving baseline agents. The authors also find that safety behavior differs across evolution surfaces and harm types, and that these differences appear in chain-of-thought reasoning, enabling a monitoring strategy that mitigates unsafe behavior with a low false positive rate.

entry.title: Revisiting dual lattice attacks on bounded distance decoding with a heuristic-free trade-off
entry.summary: Dual lattice attacks for bounded distance decoding, revisited arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 This paper examines the assumption that scores of short dual vectors in dual lattice attacks are mutually independent. In the Haar-random lattice model, without heuristic assumptions, the authors prove an explicit asymptotic trade-off between target radius and query time for decision bounded distance decoding with preprocessing. Using Siegel and Rogers moment identities, they analyze cosine scores over complete dual balls and bound error probabilities. The resulting trade-off matches the asymptotic prediction of the Ducas-Pulles conditional model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive an explicit asymptotic BDD preprocessing trade-off in the Haar-random lattice model without heuristics, which they state matches the Ducas-Pulles conditional prediction.

entry.title: An Operator-Norm Method for Security Under Quantum Advice: A Quantum Cryptography Theory Paper
entry.summary: An Operator-Norm Approach to Security with Quantum Advice arXiv · Sep 28, 2026 The paper introduces an operator-norm approach to non-uniform security in the quantum random oracle and random permutation models, giving one reduction that covers both search success probability and distinguishing advantage. The framework yields tight bounds for Yao's box with and without salting, improved bounds for pseudorandom generators, and an optimal generic salting theorem for decision games. By separating offline and online query contributions, the authors also obtain stronger bounds for salted permutation and random-function inversion.

entry.title: SKILLLITE: An evidence-guided method for auditing malicious Agent Skills using compact LLMs
entry.summary: SKILLLITE: Evidence-Guided Malicious Skill Auditing with Compact LLMs arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 Agent Skills extend LLM-based agents with task-specific instructions and executable components, but third-party Skills create a supply-chain risk because malicious ones can abuse agent privileges. The paper proposes SKILLLITE, a framework that extracts security-relevant behaviors and infers intended functionality from Skill packages, then uses a compact LLM to judge maliciousness. Experiments report improved detection across several compact LLM backbones, better results than representative baselines, generalization to in-the-wild malicious Skills, and low inference latency.

entry.title: Safer Content or Firmer Refusals? Hybrid Defense Against Harmful Fine-Tuning
entry.summary: Safer Content or Firmer Refusals? A Hybrid Perturbation Defense for Alignment under Harmful Fine-tuning arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper addresses how harmful data mixed into fine-tuning can weaken a language model's safety alignment. It proposes VaccineBooster, which combines embedding perturbation and weight-level gradient attenuation within one alignment procedure. On Llama-2-7B, it reports the lowest moderation score (0.315) while Booster-Only keeps the highest refusal rate (50%). The authors note the evaluation uses ten prompts and a single unseeded run, so the trade-off is an observed pattern rather than a statistically resolved result.
