entry.summary: A Complete Classification of Whole-Output Linear Structures in FEILIAN-Type Components IACR ePrint · Sep 27, 2026 The paper determines all input differences that give constant whole-output XOR derivatives for a four-word ARX structure containing a FEILIAN SubColumn. For any word width and XOR-linear internal maps, the linear-structure space contains a universal two-dimensional MSB family and has dimension at most five, with this bound attained. For the 64-bit FEILIAN component, the complete space equals this universal family. The results concern component structure and constancy at successive boundaries, and do not classify all endpoint structures of the iterated permutation or establish an attack on the hash.

entry.title: Lower bounds on signature length for hash-based schemes in the random oracle model
entry.summary: Lower Bounds on Random-Oracle-Model Signature Length IACR ePrint · Sep 27, 2026 The paper asks whether the large signature size of hash-based post-quantum signatures is unavoidable. Within the pure random oracle model, it proves lower bounds for schemes with non-adaptive verifiers that satisfy a property called salted soundness. For one-time signatures, the combined public key and signature length must be Ω(λ²/log λ), and for many-time signatures the signature length alone must meet this bound.

entry.title: Threshold signatures that identify who aborts, built from one-way functions
entry.summary: Threshold Signatures with Identifiable Abort from One-way Functions IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper presents a threshold signature scheme in which N participants share a signing key so that any T of them can jointly produce a valid signature. It builds on a variant of Lamport one-time signatures and Shamir secret sharing, and supports identifiable abort. The scheme is extended to multiple messages using multi-layer Merkle trees, with a bulletin board used to coordinate one-time key usage.

entry.title: One Unverified Coordinate Is Enough: Key Recovery from Faulty FO Rejection Checks in ML-KEM
entry.summary: One Unverified Coordinate Is Enough: Key Recovery from Faulty Fujisaki–Okamoto Rejection Checks in ML-KEM IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper examines what happens when the Fujisaki–Okamoto re-encryption check in ML-KEM is implemented incorrectly, as some deployed libraries reportedly do by skipping a conditional move or truncating ciphertext comparisons. The authors show that a single unverified ciphertext coordinate is enough for an attacker to recover the secret key from bounded-error observations via least squares. They prove that O(kn log kn) observations suffice under a regularity assumption and demonstrate full recovery on all three parameter sets against a simulated implementation. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report that one unverified ciphertext coordinate enables least-squares ML-KEM key recovery, prove O(kn log kn) observations identify the key, and report full recovery on a simulated incomp

entry.title: Improved attacks on local pseudorandom generators using XorMaj predicates
entry.summary: Improved Cryptanalysis of Local PRGs IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 The paper presents two seed-recovery attacks on local PRGs that apply XorMaj predicates to map an n-bit seed to an m-bit pseudorandom string. The Guess-Filter-Solve (GFS) attack extends the GAS framework and outperforms GAS, especially for short outputs. The Filter-Guess-Propagate (FGP) attack speeds up Belief Propagation compared with GADec. Both are extended to XorMod predicates and applied to a ZKP protocol and QuietOT, yielding attacks on witness indistinguishability and OT receiver privacy respectively.. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose GFS and FGP seed-recovery attacks on local PRGs, reporting far lower complexity than GAS and GADec (e.g., n=256, m=2^16) and extensions to XorMod and two protocols.

entry.title: Quantum security of XOR of permutations via Fourier analysis
entry.summary: Quantum Security of XOR of Permutations via Fourier Analysis IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper studies the quantum security of the XOR of r independent random permutations (XoP), a construction that goes beyond the birthday bound classically. The authors prove that XoP is indistinguishable from a random function for quantum algorithms making up to about 2^n/57774 queries, far beyond the quantum birthday bound. They use a Fourier-analytic polynomial method and present heuristic attacks suggesting the bounds are nearly tight. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show XOR of r≥2 random permutations is quantum beyond-birthday indistinguishable from random functions for q up to 2^n/57774, using Fourier analysis and compressed oracles, with heuristic

entry.title: Error-aware scale design for faster encrypted LLM inference
entry.summary: Error Propagation-Aware Scale Design for Efficient Homomorphic Encryption-Based LLM Inference IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper proposes a scale design for CKKS-based privacy-preserving LLM inference that accounts for how numerical errors propagate through Transformer computations. It assigns operation-wise scales and modulus levels based on the precision each operation requires, reducing unnecessary conservatism. Reported results show modulus consumption reduced by 30.0% and bootstrapping operations reduced by 83.6% versus THOR on a standard Transformer, and by 33.6% and 80% versus PowerFormer on an HE-friendly Transformer.

entry.title: TPOKÉ: A Threshold Public-Key Encryption Scheme Built on POKÉ
entry.summary: TPOKÉ: Threshold Public-Key Encryption from POKÉ via Isogeny Sharing IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper presents TPOKÉ, threshold public-key encryption schemes based on POKÉ, an efficient isogeny-based encryption scheme. The main construction, S-TPOKÉ, supports any (t,n) threshold, while Ch-TPOKÉ arranges the parties' secret isogenies in a chain for the (n,n) case. Compared with running n independent POKÉ instances, both schemes reduce the number of isogenies computed during encryption and roughly halve ciphertext size for large n.

entry.title: Operator-norm method for security with quantum advice
entry.summary: An Operator-Norm Approach to Security with Quantum Advice IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper introduces an operator-norm approach to non-uniform security in the quantum random oracle and random permutation models. It gives a unified reduction covering both search success probability and distinguishing advantage. The framework yields tighter bounds for Yao's box and pseudorandom generators, and an optimal generic salting theorem for decision games. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present a unified operator-norm framework for non-uniform security, reporting tight bounds for Yao's box and salting and improved decision-game bounds.

entry.title: Improved near-capacity lower bound for Reed-Solomon lists on multiplicative subgroups
entry.summary: An improved near-capacity lower bound for Reed-Solomon lists on multiplicative subgroups IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 The paper gives an elementary construction of large Reed-Solomon lists on multiplicative subgroups. For fixed rational rates, the leading entropy exponent of list sizes doubles the antipodal bound of Arnon, Boneh, and Fenzi. It also shows that the exponent constant c2 in the S-two whitepaper's universal list-size conjecture must be at least 2.

entry.title: Binding Humans to Keys: A Decentralized Proof of Personhood Protocol
entry.summary: Binding Humans to Keys: A Secure Decentralized Proof of Personhood Protocol IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper proposes S-GYID, a decentralized protocol that cryptographically links a digital identity to one unique living person without a trusted central authority. It replaces raw biometric transmission with an encryption-based digital fingerprint, aiming to resist identity theft and ghost key attacks. The protocol also uses a three-tier generational authority hierarchy with bounded tenure and VRF-based session selection to limit collusion. The authors prove resistance properties under standard cryptographic assumptions and provide a hypergeometric analysis for setting parameters.

entry.title: Geometric Forgeries: Structural Cryptanalysis of MAYO. A paper attacking the post-quantum signature scheme MAYO by exploiting its underlying mathematical structure.
entry.summary: Geometric Forgeries: Structural Cryptanalysis of MAYO IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 MAYO is a post-quantum signature scheme based on UOV that uses whipping to make public keys more compact. The paper presents the first structural forgery attack exploiting the geometry of its multivariate quadratic maps, combined with the Pseudo-Oil Attack and a descent to the binary field. It also introduces a multi-target reduction for homogeneous MQ maps. The authors report that these attacks lower the estimated bit security of MAYO Round 2 Levels I and III by about 18 and 16 bits, with Level I falling 15 bits short, and reduce estimated security of the Round 3 parameters, leaving MAYO2 3 bits below its required level. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first forgery attack exploiting the geometry induced by MAYO's whipping transformation, plus a multi-target reduction for homogeneous MQ maps; they report Round 2 Level I falli

entry.title: SUCRE: a masking countermeasure that protects ML-DSA rejection sampling from physical attacks
entry.summary: ML-DSA masking sweetened with SUCRE: Shuffle-and-Unmask Countermeasure for REjection sampling IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper presents SUCRE, a countermeasure that physically protects the rejection sampling step of ML-DSA, a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature scheme. Its masking gadget unmasks a vector while randomly permuting its coefficients, preserving the infinity norm so rejection sampling works without complex mask conversions. The authors give a formal proof against d-probing adversaries, based on a new MLWR variant with a concrete security analysis. The implementation runs four to six times faster than Coron et al. (TCHES 2024), at the cost of higher memory usage. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose SUCRE, which unmasks while randomly permuting coefficients to protect ML-DSA rejection sampling; they give a d-probing proof and an MLWR variant analysis, reporting 4-6x speedup ov

entry.title: Cyclotomic Cosets: a quantum sieve for hidden subgroups with prime-power moduli
entry.summary: Cyclotomic Cosets: Hidden Subgroup and Quantum Sieving Algorithm for Prime-Power Moduli IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper studies the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem, a basis of post-quantum cryptography, by introducing the Cyclotomic Coset Problem (CCP), a cyclotomic generalization of the Dihedral Coset Problem that keeps an exact hidden-subgroup structure. The authors use a π-adic ideal chain in cyclotomic rings to build a quantum sieve that reduces phase states step by step. For fixed prime p and modulus q=p^t, they report solving CCP in time and sample complexity 2^{O_p(log n log q)}, with extensions to uniform EDCP and Gaussian cases. The authors state that this result alone does not yield a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm for standard LWE. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce the Cyclotomic Coset Problem and a π-adic quantum sieve extending power-of-two EDCP results to prime-power moduli, reporting quasi-polynomial time when q=poly(n) but not directly

entry.title: Decryption failures in NGCC lattice KEMs under correlated blocks and omitted noise
entry.summary: Decryption Failures in NGCC Lattice KEMs: Correlated Blocks, Omitted Compression Noise, and Failure Boosting under a Query Cap IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper recomputes decryption failure probabilities for several lattice KEMs submitted to China's NGCC post-quantum competition. It examines three mechanisms: correlated decoding blocks, compression noise omitted from Cheetah's specification, and bounded noise in two-dimensional codes used by Rudraksh2 and Scabbard. The authors report that several estimated failure costs fall below nominal security levels under a 2^80 query cap. No key recovery attack is described. ★★★★ Notable: Identifies three decryption-failure mechanisms in NGCC lattice KEMs (correlated blocks, omitted compression noise, bounded 2D-code noise) and reports recomputed failure rates, with estimated costs bel

entry.title: Adaptively UC-secure oblivious transfer built from group actions
entry.summary: Adaptively UC-Secure Oblivious Transfer from Group Actions IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper presents the first adaptively UC-secure oblivious transfer protocol based on group actions, assuming weakly pseudorandom effective group actions such as CSIDH. The receiver learns exactly one of the sender's two messages without revealing its choice. The authors follow the BC15 framework and address the lack of SPHF-friendly IND-CCA encryption from group actions by building a verifiable chameleon hash and a publicly verifiable scheme in the random oracle model.

entry.title: Batch decryption under new standard assumptions
entry.summary: Batch Decryption from New Standard Assumptions IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper studies batch decryption, where an authority releases a short key allowing public decryption of a chosen batch of ciphertexts, motivated by encrypted mempools. It gives two constructions with different authorization semantics and assumptions. The first is an epochless RSA-group scheme based on Fiat's Batch RSA, with a single-group-element hint, proven adaptively secure under the strong RSA assumption in the random-oracle model. The second is a generic epoch-based identity-based encryption construction, instantiated from the computational Diffie-Hellman assumption. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give an RSA-group batch decryption scheme with no batch bound fixed at setup and size independent of batch size, reporting adaptive security under strong RSA; they also present an epoch-ba

entry.title: Generic-group bounds for multi-instance problems, focusing on Inverse Diffie-Hellman
entry.summary: Generic Bounds for Multi-Instance Problems: The Strange Case of Inverse Diffie-Hellman IACR ePrint · Sep 28, 2026 This paper studies how hard multi-instance problems over prime-order groups are in the generic group model, where an adversary must solve at least k of n independent instances. It shows that multi-instance CDH and SDH are as hard as solving k independent discrete logarithms, while multi-instance IDH and LKDH can be significantly easier than multi-instance CDH in certain parameter regimes. All these problems offer 1/2(log(p)+log(k)) bits of security. The lower bounds extend Yun's hyperplane query model and are derived using algebraic geometry techniques. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give generic-group bounds for multi-instance problems, report that multi-instance IDH can be significantly easier than CDH in some regimes, and extend Yun's hyperplane query model.

entry.title: AEBAP: An efficient elliptic-curve-based authentication protocol for wireless networks
entry.summary: AEBAP: An Efficient ECC-Based Authentication Protocol Designed for Wireless Networks IACR ePrint · Sep 29, 2026 This paper proposes AEBAP, an authentication protocol based on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) designed for secure communication in resource-constrained IoT environments. It aims to provide mutual authentication, data integrity, and resistance to passive and active attacks. The authors evaluate performance through experimental implementation and analyze security using informal reasoning and formal verification tools, Scyther and ProVerif. The paper reports strong security with minimal computational and communication overhead.

entry.title: Improved differential-linear attacks on Orthros, Gleeok, ZIP-AES and ZIP-GIFT
entry.summary: Improved Differential-Linear Cryptanalysis of Orthros, Gleeok, ZIP-AES, and ZIP-GIFT IACR ePrint · Sep 29, 2026 This paper improves differential-linear distinguishers and gives key-recovery attacks on reduced-round versions of several pseudorandom functions. It extends the analyzed coverage of Orthros from 7 to 9 rounds and of Gleeok-128 from 4 to 5 rounds. The authors use automated differential and linear trail search together with existing round-based correlation estimation.

entry.title: Factoring RSA Moduli via Affine-Padded Rabin Oracles at Special-Sieve Cost
entry.summary: Affine-Padding Rabin-Oracle Factoring in L_nleft(frac13,√[3]frac329right) IACR ePrint · Sep 29, 2026 This paper revisits the Joux-Naccache-Thomé construction for the Rabin case (e=2), using an affine-padded square-root oracle that returns a single canonical root. The authors use a one-sided number field sieve to obtain congruences of squares that split the modulus with probability 1/2 per dependency, claiming complexity L_n(1/3, (32/9)^(1/3)), below the general sieve. An open-source implementation is said to confirm a performance improvement in factoring speed.

entry.title: Machine-Checked Soundness Proof of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates
entry.summary: Machine-Checked Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates arXiv · Oct 5, 2026 This paper machine-checks in Isabelle/HOL the soundness of the GKR protocol for sparse-Merkle membership, non-membership and update proofs, together with arithmetization exactness and leaf-commitment binding. It proves that for a false output claim, the probability that a layered sumcheck accepts a false result is at most (s_out + Σ(2 s_i d_i + 1))/|F|. The bound is instantiated over a quartic extension of the 31-bit KoalaBear field, giving a denominator of about 2^124. The model covers only the interactive public-coin protocol and excludes Fiat-Shamir, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge.

entry.title: Paper arguing peer review should limit evaluative authority
entry.summary: Peer review should constrain evaluative authority arXiv · Oct 2, 2026 This paper argues that peer-review reform should shift from improving evaluators or aggregating judgments to constraining evaluative authority under persistent uncertainty. It proposes authority-constrained peer review, requiring consequential judgments to pass structured scrutiny before being treated as decision-relevant. Proposed mechanisms include critique-authority decoupling, independent secondary evaluation, contestability and reversibility, and accountability for unsupported influence.

entry.title: Aligning models by training against probes while keeping them monitorable
entry.summary: Alignment via Training Against Probes Without Losing Monitorability arXiv · Sep 30, 2026 This paper studies probe-guided fine-tuning, which uses probes that detect undesired properties in model activations as a direct training signal. It evaluates harmlessness and honesty objectives, finding that static probes are easily exploited while continuously updated probes reduce harmfulness and improve honesty while preserving utility. The method outperforms DPO and inference-time steering and is more robust to jailbreak and abliteration attacks. Concepts remain linearly encoded after fine-tuning, so oversight is preserved.

entry.title: Not Self-Decidable: Why LLMs Cannot Set the Limits of What an Agent Verifier Can Check
entry.summary: Not Self-Decidable: LLMs Cannot Draw the Boundary of What an Agent Verifier Can Check arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 The paper studies how an agent verifier should separate rules that a fixed check can settle from rules that need a judge. Across six corpora, about 22,000 labels from four models show near-perfect agreement on obvious cases but divergent, opposite-direction errors on regulatory text, and shared over-claiming on a deployed credit agent's rules. The authors propose CoVer, which admits a predicate only if its synthesized check survives intervention, reads fields the agent cannot write, and holds under deterministic rewording. They argue self-decidability is a boundary the verifier must construct, not a capability to elicit from a model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report from about 22,000 labels across six corpora that LLMs cannot self-determine an agent verifier's decidable boundary, and propose CoVer, which admits a predicate only if its synthesiz

entry.title: Penumbra: Efficient adversarial search for finding where regulatory rules flip
entry.summary: Penumbra: Sample-Efficient Adversarial Search for Regulatory Obligations arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 The paper introduces Penumbra, an adversarial search method for regulatory red-teaming that starts from a verified compliant response and expands edits until a two-evaluator committee changes its verdict. It outputs pairs of adjacent responses on opposite sides of the compliance boundary. Tested on a financial advisory constitution and a clinical triage constitution, it returned 144 and 49 pairs respectively, often differing by only a few words.

entry.title: COPEX: Testing how well LLMs resist harmful context across MCP layers
entry.summary: COPEX: Benchmarking LLM Robustness to Adversarial Context Across Model Context Protocol (MCP) Layers arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper presents COPEX, a benchmark that isolates the language model as the MCP client by fixing the surrounding agent stack and varying only the tool-selecting model. It covers 25 attack types across 125 scenarios spanning four entry surfaces: model/agent, client, server/tool, and transport. Across nine models and 3,375 trials, the mean attack success rate is 64.4%. Combined input and context scanning reduced mean attack success by 49.6% on an eight-attack defense subset compared with the undefended setting.} ★★★★ Notable: Isolates the model as MCP client in a controlled benchmark of 125 adversarial context scenarios and 3,375 trials, reporting a 49.6% drop in attack success with input and context scanning.

entry.title: CHAMP: A Cayley Hash Built from 2×2 Matrix Products
entry.summary: CHAMP: Cayley HAshing with Matrix Products arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 Cayley hash functions map binary strings to values by treating message bits as semigroup elements and multiplying them, which yields useful homomorphic properties. This paper proposes CHAMP, a Cayley hash function based on products of 2 by 2 matrices over a finite field. It discusses the scheme's security, implementation, and performance.

entry.title: Rethinking Quality in LLM Routing: Security-Aware Model and Budget Selection
entry.summary: Rethinking Quality in Large Language Model Routing: Security-Conditioned Model-and-Budget Selection arXiv · Oct 14, 2026 This paper introduces SCRouter, a router that chooses which large language model to call and how many output tokens to allow for each query. It weighs answer utility for ordinary queries against security behavior, such as refusing harmful requests, for sensitive ones, then balances the result against cost. The authors also release SCRouterBench, containing 38,869 in-domain queries across nine security dimensions and 2,753 out-of-domain queries, each evaluated under 144 model-budget combinations. The paper reports that SCRouter outperforms baselines by 13 to 29 points in-domain and 19 to 23 points out-of-domain.

entry.title: Receipts for Tool Agents: Binding Claims, Evidence, and Execution for Auditing
entry.summary: Actions with Receipts: Jointly Binding Claims, Evidence, and Execution for Replayable Tool-Agent Auditing arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 The paper addresses a gap in tool-using AI agents, where citations and execution logs may each look valid while a shown claim is not the one produced by the recorded execution or supported by the cited source. The authors propose a claim-anchored execution contract that jointly binds the emitted claim, its exact source span, the ordered execution prefix, and the source version and access state. A deterministic verifier checks these bindings separately from a support check. Across 1,280 cross-object attacks, the joint contract detected 1,275 substitutions (0.9961).

entry.title: VStress: Auditing and Budgeting Repeated Verifier Calls by Correlation
entry.summary: VStress: Correlation-Aware Auditing and Adaptive Budget Allocation for Repeated Verifiers arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 The paper introduces VStress, an auditable replay contract, and VStress-CA, a correlation-aware policy that decides whether another verifier call adds conditional information and stops or abstains when it does not. In controlled tests, majority voting helped at 35% symmetric corruption but lost accuracy at 65%. At a matched fixed budget, VStress-CA achieved the highest balanced accuracy among the compared allocation methods. Dependence diagnostics rose from same-model repeats to cross-family channels.

entry.title: Automated Detection of Open-Source Software Threats Using Taxonomy-Aligned Large Language Models
entry.summary: Autonomous OSS Threat Detection via Taxonomy-Aligned LLMs arXiv · Oct 1, 2026 This paper proposes a large language model framework that automatically detects and classifies open-source software supply chain threats into five attack categories. The authors build a dataset of 999 verified real-world incidents from 2018 to 2026 across eight package ecosystems. Using taxonomy-aligned prompting with GPT-4, the framework reports 97% accuracy and 97% macro F1, and the authors find taxonomy alignment matters more than model scale or fine-tuning.

entry.title: Privacy Foundations for Shared Scientific AI: A Framework for Stating and Auditing Claims
entry.summary: Privacy Foundations for Multi-Institutional Scientific Artificial Intelligence arXiv · Sep 30, 2026 This paper examines privacy risks as scientific AI is shared among national laboratories, universities, hospitals, and industry partners. It argues that existing tools such as differential privacy and federated learning protect only parts of the system, and their guarantees rarely combine across institutions. The authors propose a six-element framework (protected asset, observer, channel, permitted disclosure, guarantee, and evidence) for stating, comparing, and auditing privacy claims, and identify six research priorities.

entry.title: SecJev: Security-specialized decision models for System One tasks
entry.summary: SecJev: Bringing Security Expertise to System One Decision Models arXiv · Oct 2, 2026 This paper introduces SecJev, described as the first family of Jev-style decision models specialized for security, with sizes from 0.8B to 9B parameters. Built on Kev's single-pass candidate scorer, it learns Boolean, choice, and ordered decisions from text, telemetry, and observation histories, trained on the newly built SecJev-Corpus spanning 14 tasks and eight sources. The authors report that SecJev-0.8B outperforms general Kev-9B by 20.51 percentage points in task-macro accuracy.

entry.title: Adaptive Co-Serving LLM Watermarking on Modern Inference Engines: a study co-designing LLM watermarks with inference infrastructure to balance quality, detectability, and serving efficiency.
entry.summary: Adaptive Co-Serving LLM Watermarking on Modern Inference Engines arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 The paper notes that existing LLM watermarking methods focus on algorithms and often add auxiliary models or external tools, which increases latency and memory use. It proposes SWIFT, which integrates generation and watermark construction in a shared backend, runs watermarking concurrently through asynchronous co-serving and adaptive scheduling, and uses vLLM optimizations. Reported results include a utility score of 4.87, 99.65% detection accuracy versus 76.65% for SynthID, up to 97.7% detection under watermark removal attacks, and 5.9x lower latency than SafeSeal.

entry.title: Control OSWorld: A Safety Test Environment for AI Agents That Use Computer Interfaces
entry.summary: Control OSWorld: An AI Control Environment for GUI Computer Use Agents arXiv · Oct 2, 2026 This paper introduces Control OSWorld, an evaluation environment that pairs 318 OSWorld tasks with 81 harmful side tasks, such as exfiltrating a private file, that an agent must complete without being caught. The authors use it to study monitors that detect malicious agents operating a graphical user interface. A weaker monitor reliably separates honest from malicious trajectories when it sees the full trajectory, reaching 97% recall at a 3% false positive rate. When it must score each step before execution, recall drops at low false positive rates, and access to the agent's visible text matters more than screenshots.

entry.title: Measuring GPS Spoofing of Ships at Sea Worldwide
entry.summary: She Spoofed Sea Ships by the Sea Shore: Measuring Large-Scale GPS Spoofing in Global Maritime Traffic arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper presents the first large-scale study of GPS spoofing in maritime traffic, using global ship tracking (AIS) data. The authors detect groups of vessels whose reported positions jump in physically implausible, correlated ways, and grade the evidence in each region. Analyzing over 367,000 vessels from late November 2024 to early February 2025, they identify 31 persistent anomalous hotspots, at least 22 with strong evidence of spoofing. The study also reports spoofing in the Red Sea months before the MSC Antonia grounding, which had not been documented previously. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first large-scale measurement of maritime GPS spoofing, using a motion-aware regional detector on AIS data from over 367,000 vessels. They report 31 persistent hotspots, at lea

entry.title: Layer-Resolved Measurement of LLM Agent Defenses and an Envelope-Layer Attack-Defense Model
entry.summary: Measuring LLM Agent Defenses by Layer: GDA Measurement and an Envelope-Layer Attack-Defense Model arXiv · Sep 30, 2026 This paper studies indirect prompt injection in agent protocols such as ACP and A2A, where remote tasks may be treated as legitimate. It argues that attack success rate cannot show which layer needs strengthening, and proposes GDA Measurement, which sorts outcomes into four classes. It also introduces A2A-TIBA for generating a validation corpus and ELA-ITL, a three-layer model, and reports that annotating untrusted content markedly improves recognition of malicious content.

entry.title: Riemannian Transform Curbs Cross-Session Identity Leakage in Motor-Imagery EEG
entry.summary: Riemannian Suppression of Cross-Session Identity Leakage in Motor-Imagery EEG arXiv · Oct 11, 2026 Motor-imagery EEG recordings carry subject-identifying structure that persists across sessions, so sessions from the same person can be linked. This paper proposes a Riemannian transform that works directly on covariance representations by equalizing subject-conditioned geometric statistics, without learning a privacy model. Across two public datasets, the worst-case attacker's identification rate drops substantially, with a moderate loss in motor-imagery decoding accuracy.

entry.title: A symmetric cipher built on Dirichlet convolution over finite fields
entry.summary: Symmetric Cryptography via Dirichlet Convolution arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper proposes a new symmetric-key cipher for encrypting digital data, claiming fast operation, low memory use, and resistance to classical, AI-assisted, and quantum attacks. The scheme is based on generalized Dirichlet convolution over finite fields and is analyzed for security against plaintext attacks from an information-theoretic view. Its nonlocal structure permits plaintext salting, allowing controlled key reuse. The authors state that over F_p with p>2 the cipher achieves information-theoretic security under key reuse, while over F_2 some information leakage remains, giving a finite key-reuse budget.

entry.title: Building Trustworthy Household Robots Through Open-World Safety
entry.summary: Building Trustworthy Household Robots through Open-World Safety arXiv · Oct 1, 2026 This position paper argues that foundation models let household robots handle more objects and instructions, but cluttered, changing homes expose them to unfamiliar situations. The authors call for open-world safety, meaning robots should keep specified safety requirements even in unseen situations, including when they cannot complete a task. They propose a research agenda to specify, learn, and ground safety requirements, enforce them with reliable recovery, and evaluate how well these protections generalize.

entry.title: Argos: A Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture for Coordinating Distributed Edge Security Devices
entry.summary: Argos: A Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture for Distributed Edge Security Orchestration arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper presents Argos, a multi-tenant SaaS command-and-control architecture for transparently and automatically managing distributed edge devices over the long term. It provides role-based access control, tenant isolation, persistent task management, and cron-based workflow automation. The system was tested on three geographically distributed edge devices running 810 automated tasks mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, with a global failure rate of 3.33%. The evaluation methodology, sanitized datasets, and statistical scripts are publicly available.

entry.title: Key-reuse weakness in phase-keyed Fourier-curve modulation: leakage and key-refresh cost on coded links
entry.summary: Key-Reuse Vulnerability of Phase-Keyed Fourier-Curve Modulation: Relation Leakage and Key-Refresh Cost on Coded Links arXiv · Oct 1, 2026 The paper argues that judging such keyed modulation by key-space size and a keyless receiver's error rate is insufficient, since reusing keys with harmonically coupled waveforms leaks information. Using integer relations among harmonic indices, the authors build an attack that recovers the key without enumeration. With one key per codeword on an LDPC-coded link, the attack meets a predeclared compromise criterion at most tested operating points. The paper also evaluates artificial noise countermeasures and the key cost of different refresh schedules.

entry.title: Aletheia: Permission-Minimality Testing for Coding-Agent Rules
entry.summary: Aletheia: Permission-Minimality Testing for Coding-Agent Rules arXiv · Sep 30, 2026 This paper presents Aletheia, a framework that tests whether the permissions requested by coding-agent rule files, such as AGENTS.md and Cursor rules, are actually needed to complete a task. It removes one permission at a time, re-runs the task in a restricted sandbox, and flags the rule as suspicious if the task still passes its functional tests. On the evaluated sets, it detected all 314 attack rules and produced three false positives among 85 benign rules.

entry.title: Evaluating and Improving Large Language Model Robustness to Adversarial Input Variations
entry.summary: Evaluating and Improving the Robustness of Large Language Models to Input Sequence Variations arXiv · Oct 2, 2026 This thesis studies how robust large language models are against adversarial input changes such as prompt injections, backdoors, and manipulation of automatic quality metrics. It proposes R_stab(f), a generative robustness metric based on Jensen-Shannon divergence, and ASA, an adaptive black-box attack on LLM-as-a-Judge systems reaching up to 73.8% attack success rate. It also introduces AttestMCP, which attests tool calls in agentic systems, reducing average attack success rate on the 847-scenario MCPBench from 53.7% to 12.4%. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes the JS-divergence-based generative robustness metric R_stab(f), the adaptive attack ASA, and AttestMCP, reporting ASR falling from 53.7% to 12.4% on MCPBench.

entry.title: Pretext: A Method That Evades Malicious Skill Detectors for AI Agents
entry.summary: Pretext: Defeating Malicious Skill Detection Frameworks for AI Agents arXiv · Sep 30, 2026 This paper examines the risk that malicious skills, which inject instructions into an AI agent's context, can be used to attack agents. The authors present Pretext, a white-box LLM attacker that iteratively crafts skills that evade pre-installation scanners while still delivering the payload and performing the benign task. Across three open-source models, Pretext reaches up to 97% evasion against a frozen detector and 77% against a co-adaptive one, exposing major gaps in current skill scanners.

entry.title: APEX: Active Defense at LLM Agent Execution Boundaries (Paper)
entry.summary: APEX: Active Protection at Execution Boundaries for LLM Agents arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper addresses indirect prompt injection, where hidden instructions in content read by LLM agents at runtime can trigger harmful actions. It proposes defending at the execution boundary, where an agent turns internal state into external actions or outputs, using an authorization contract compiled before untrusted execution. APEX admits effects only when the contract justifies them and exposes unendorsed use before the effect commits. The authors report 0% attack success on five of six benchmarks and 0.56% on the sixth, compared against 13 baselines. ★★★★★ Notable: Shifts defense to execution boundaries, enforcing one authorization contract via evidence gating and deception-based exposure; the authors report 0% attack success on five of six benchmarks (0.56% on

entry.title: SERA-IDS: Intrusion detection using small language models that learn from structured past experience
entry.summary: SERA-IDS: Structured Experience Retrieval-Augmented Intrusion Detection with Small Language Models arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 The paper proposes SERA-IDS, a framework in which a small language model learns structured rules from misclassified network flows. At test time, rules matching the query flow's numerical conditions are retrieved and supplied as evidence. Using three locally deployable small models without fine-tuning, the authors report large macro F1 gains on the NF-BoT-IoT and NF-ToN-IoT datasets.

entry.title: Do LLM Extraction Defenses Hold Up Against Different Attacks? A Benchmark for Black-Box Model Extraction
entry.summary: Do Defenses Against LLM Extraction Work Across Attacks? A Lifecycle Benchmark of Black-Box Model Extraction arXiv · Oct 1, 2026 The paper introduces a unified benchmark covering six extraction attacks, ten defenses, and two adaptive attacks that paraphrase or back-translate protected responses before training surrogates. It controls model configurations, query data, budgets, and evaluation conditions within each comparison. Measurements include surrogate capability, fidelity to the victim, output quality via Rep-4, and sensitivity to query budget.

entry.title: Which image property carries image-to-text jailbreaks? A controlled breakdown of attack factors
entry.summary: Which Image Property Carries the Jailbreak? A Controlled Dissection of Image-to-Text Jailbreaks arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 The paper examines image-side factors in four published image-to-text jailbreak attack families, using a 313-prompt StrongREJECT slice and five multimodal models, plus an appendix evaluation of InternVL3.5-8B. Bare harmful text queries produce little attack success, while attack images substantially increase it. Per-tile entropy and JPEG size do not reliably separate attack tiles from size-matched benign distractors, and removing query-specific relatedness lowers attack success by about 0.12 on Qwen3-VL-8B. The conclusions remain conditional on an automated rubric judge.

entry.title: Where the audio jailbreak lives: a controlled frequency and depth audit of AdvWave-P on Qwen2-Audio
entry.summary: Where Does the Audio Jailbreak Live? A Controlled Frequency-Depth Audit of AdvWave-P on Qwen2-Audio arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper audits claims about which frequency bands and decoder layers matter for AdvWave-P, an additive audio jailbreak attack on Qwen2-Audio. The authors mask frequency components of the perturbation in the STFT domain and measure attack success on 520 AdvBench prompts, with 76.7% of adversarial inputs judged as jailbreaks. They find the apparent frequency ranking depends on how bands are partitioned, and a finer-resolution result remains unresolved without a matched control. The authors conclude the results support partition-aware auditing of frequency claims, but the layer association is not a causal localization.

entry.title: TARE: Measuring a Never-Poisoned Twin to Assess Backdoor-Defense Costs
entry.summary: TARE: Weigh a Never-Poisoned Twin Before Reading Backdoor-Defense Costs arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 Backdoor-defense leaderboards report clean-accuracy drops as removal costs, but these drops mix in the defense's effect on any model and the victim's starting point. The paper proposes TARE, which runs each defense on a never-poisoned twin sharing the same recipe, schedule and seed, and treats the twin's loss as the "tare" to subtract. The authors also release a patch, a signed tare table, and TARE-Z, a twin-free estimator for seed-stable defenses. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a never-poisoned twin baseline to correct backdoor-defense accuracy cost; a 2×2 scheduler swap exposes a benchmark flaw, and BadNets results on the twin are reported for eight defenses.

entry.title: ASAP: Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode Refinement for Binary Decompilation
entry.summary: ASAP: Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode Refinement For Binary Decompilation arXiv · Sep 30, 2026 Binary decompilers produce C-like pseudocode that is heuristic and often contains errors, especially for heavily optimized binaries. ASAP aligns source and assembly representations with contrastive learning, compresses assembly features into fixed tokens via a Q-Former, and feeds them with the pseudocode to an LLM. Stochastic pseudocode masking and a relative assembly-advantage loss encourage the model to use assembly information. On two benchmarks, average re-execution rate rises from 64.7% to 71.9% and recompilation rate from 91.6% to 96.6% over the strongest baseline.

entry.title: Unitary Complexity in Polynomial Space
entry.summary: Unitary complexity in polynomial space arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 The paper shows that if quantum commitments exist, then either unitary synthesis has no polynomial-time solution or BPP is not equal to NEXP. It proposes new definitions for the unitary complexity classes unitaryP and unitaryPSPACE. It also shows that unitaryPSPACE can generically erase garbage qubits. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show that if quantum commitments exist, then either unitary synthesis has no polynomial-time solution or BPP≠NEXP, and propose new definitions of unitaryP and unitaryPSPACE.

entry.title: Quantum Fire with Delegated Cloning: A cryptographic primitive where copying quantum states needs a separate key
entry.summary: Quantum Fire with Delegated Cloning arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper studies quantum fire, quantum states that can be cloned efficiently but resist reconstruction from classical communication alone. The authors introduce delegatable quantum fire, in which cloning requires a separate key, and give two constructions in the classical-oracle model. The first uses a classical secret key, while the second, called torch-fire, uses quantum cloning keys (torches) that enable cloning without being splittable or delegable. The authors claim that an efficient adversary with m torches cannot, except with negligible probability, let more than m non-communicating parties each clone a fresh challenge flame.

entry.title: Research on quantum interactive proofs where the prover sends very short replies
entry.summary: On quantum interactive proofs with a laconic prover arXiv · Sep 30, 2026 This paper studies two-message quantum interactive proof systems in which the prover's response is only ℓ bits long. The authors introduce the class QIP_{ℓ-bit}(2) and show that Quantum State Distinguishability is complete for it, placing it just above quantum statistical zero-knowledge (QSZK). They also identify easy regimes where the class collapses to QSZK. Under quantum public coins, the interaction is shown to be useless, with the relevant class contained in BQP. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a complete multi-state distinguishability characterization of QIP_ℓ-bit(2), report that QSD lies in QSZK when a-b≥1/O(log n), and improve results for SD and SZK.

entry.title: Succinct arguments for QMA in the quantum random oracle model
entry.summary: Succinct Arguments for QMA in the Quantum Random Oracle Model arXiv · Sep 29, 2026 This paper constructs the first succinct argument for QMA in the quantum random oracle model (QROM), without relying on additional cryptographic assumptions or unproven conjectures. The core is an efficiency-preserving transformation that compiles quantum interactive oracle proofs (QIOPs) into quantum arguments for the same language, using a quantum commit-and-open paradigm. The authors also formalize and construct extractable vector commitments for quantum states with local openings in the QROM. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first succinct argument for QMA in the QROM relying only on unstructured hardness, via an efficiency-preserving QIOP-to-argument compilation and extractable vector commitments f

entry.title: The Poisoned Conversation: Privacy-Leaking Watermarks in Unified Multimodal Models explains how hidden image watermarks can leak sensitive chat information.
entry.summary: The Poisoned Conversation: Privacy-Leaking Watermarks in Unified Multimodal Models arXiv · Oct 5, 2026 The paper introduces Privacy-Leaking Watermarks (PLWs), invisible watermarks that a malicious model provider can embed in later generated images based on earlier chat history. Sensitive keywords mentioned in a conversation can thus be revealed through images, even when the model runs locally on a user's device. Tested across 13 sensitive-attribute triggers and two model families, PLWs achieved up to 100.0% true positive rate at 1% false positive rate.

entry.title: AutoDP-LLM: Using Large Language Models to Automate Data Pre-processing for Intrusion Detection
entry.summary: AutoDP-LLM: Automating Data Pre-processing for Intrusion Detection Systems using Large Language Models arXiv · Oct 5, 2026 This paper proposes AutoDP-LLM, a framework that uses Large Language Models to automatically generate and validate executable data pre-processing pipelines for intrusion detection systems. It selects retained features adaptively using semantic reasoning and training-derived statistics, without a predefined feature budget. Experiments on the UNSW-NB15 and NSL-KDD datasets show competitive detection performance compared with conventional feature-selection methods. The authors also note that the candidate pipeline generation and evaluation steps can run in parallel on high-performance computing systems.

entry.title: Reflections and Fragments: Defending LLMs Against Multi-Turn Mosaic Attacks
entry.summary: Reflections and Fragments: Securing LLMs Against Sequential Mosaic Attacks arXiv · Oct 5, 2026 This paper studies mosaic attacks, where individually harmless prompts across several conversation turns combine into a harmful payload. The authors propose a watchman, an online state mechanism that carries safety-relevant information forward, and show that under explicit assumptions it can achieve zero-failure defense with positive benign helpfulness. In experiments, role-specific attacker and defender LoRA adapters trained via multi-turn self-play over frozen LLMs both improved, with gains also observed on unseen attack objectives.

entry.title: Grammar-guided code watermarking with green temperature (GTCW), a method to tag AI-generated code while keeping it syntactically valid
entry.summary: Grammar-Guided Code Watermarking with Green Temperature arXiv · Oct 5, 2026 This paper proposes GTCW, a method that embeds a detectable watermark in code generated by large language models. At each decoding step it limits candidates to grammar-valid tokens, splits them into keyed green and red sets, and reweights green tokens at high-entropy positions. Across five models and five benchmarks in four programming languages, it reaches a mean AUROC of 73.61%, above the strongest baseline's 67.83%. Its mean Pass@1 is 59.18%, slightly below the 59.58% of unwatermarked generation.

entry.title: Red-TTT: Test-time training to automatically jailbreak large language models
entry.summary: Red-TTT: Test-Time Training for Automated Jailbreaking Large Language Models arXiv · Oct 5, 2026 This paper proposes Red-TTT, a method for automated jailbreaking of large language models that updates the attacker's parameters during each attack. Each round, the attacker samples candidates, scores them against the victim's replies, and takes a policy-gradient step, and the training objective is adapted to judge success by the best sample. At a budget of 120 samples, average attack success rate rises from 55.9% for the Best-of-N baseline to 72.4%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply test-time training to automated jailbreaking, updating attacker weights during each attack; they report average success rising from 55.9% (Best-of-N) to 72.4% at 120 samples.

entry.title: Whose Interests Does a Proactive Agent Serve? Provider-Side Indirect Prompt Injection
entry.summary: Who Is Your Agent Serving? Provider-Side Indirect Prompt Injection in Proactive Agents arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper studies how an external provider could exploit proactive personal agents that make recommendations and offer follow-up help to steer users toward the provider's own target. The authors describe three mechanisms, Target Control, Private Binding, and Prospective Support, and test them across three environments and six simulated user models. The full attack raised target authorization in every tested combination, with a macro gain of up to 77.4 percentage points. The work concludes that capabilities built to serve users can be redirected toward objectives outside the user-agent relationship. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces provider-side indirect prompt injection in proactive agents, where controlling only target-related content redirects agents toward the provider's goal, reportedly raising target authorizati

entry.title: What a policy gate can and cannot know: limits of cross-platform command adjudication
entry.summary: What a Policy Gate Can and Cannot Know: Measured Boundaries of Cross-Platform Command Adjudication arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 The paper studies a policy gate that decides ALLOW, ASK or DENY from a typed, realised action without parsing shell syntax, replicating an earlier Windows benchmark on Linux. A frozen 61-case table passed fully with no false allows, and the mutation campaign killed 46 of 50 mutants (92.0%). When consulted by the executor, 25 escapes dropped to zero without blocking any benign payload. The authors also report that credential verification scans its entire ledger, incurring accumulating cost, and describe the fix they would make.

entry.title: Blocking Staged Prompt Injection Before Harmful Agent Actions
entry.summary: Blocking at the Boundary: Auditing Long-Horizon Agents against Staged Prompt Injection arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper studies how long-horizon AI agents can be attacked by indirect prompt injection spread across multiple workflow stages. The authors built an automated attack pipeline and found confirmed attacks against Claude Code and Codex across several scenarios. They propose a pre-action auditing method, Path-Aligned Attribution (PAA), which is training-free and decides Pass or Block before a consequential action takes effect, reporting higher block recall and lower false-block rates than compared auditors. ★★★★★ Notable: Introduces staged prompt injection and Path-Aligned Attribution, a training-free pre-action auditor; the abstract reports 86% Block recall at 6-8% false-block rate on a 479-pair benchmark, above ARGUS

entry.title: VulValidate: Checking Function-Level Vulnerability Labels with Executable Evidence
entry.summary: VulValidate: Auditing Function-Level Vulnerability Labels with Executable Evidence arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 Learning-based vulnerability detectors need accurate labels, but datasets built from vulnerability-fixing commits can mark functions as vulnerable just because a security patch changed them. VulValidate uses LLM agents to coordinate dynamic analysis tools and build vulnerability-triggering experiments from runtime feedback. The authors audited 35,849 instances labeled vulnerable in BigVul, PrimeVul, and DiverseVul, confirming 20,510, correcting 6,819 labels, leaving 7,981 undecided, and failing to measure 539. Corrected labels lowered F1 for all five tested detectors under fixed parameters. ★★★★★ Notable: LLM agents coordinate dynamic analysis to audit 35,849 labels across three vulnerability datasets with executable evidence; the authors report 20,510 confirmed, 6,819 corrected, and F1 gains after ret

entry.title: Private component-by-component learning: a differentially private framework for realizable settings
entry.summary: Private Component-by-Component Learning arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper studies differentially private learning where hypotheses are specified by k components in a realizable setting. It uses the LabelBoost procedure to restore exact realizability and recycles data through two alternating reservoirs, keeping overhead to roughly √k/ε. Applied to learning d-dimensional halfspaces on a finite grid, it improves the sample complexity bound, and it also yields proper private learners for Boolean compositions of classes.

entry.title: Cooldown Landmines: Cross-tenant attacks that disrupt shared LLM model access
entry.summary: Cooldown Landmines: Cross-Tenant Interference Attacks on LLM Gateways arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper studies how shared cooldown records in LLM gateways can let one tenant's request failures restrict other tenants' access to working model deployments. The authors identify two attacks against LiteLLM and propose an origin check plus tenant-scoped cooldown as fixes. In their experiments, victim fallback after recovery dropped from 54/60 to 0/60 with tenant scoping.

entry.title: How known open-source vulnerabilities affect security inside AI agent systems
entry.summary: Characterizing Security Effects of OSS Vulnerabilities in Agent Systems arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 Software agents increasingly rely on open-source components when running tools and interacting with external systems, so flaws in those dependencies can spread through tool outputs, agent state, and information shown to the model. The paper studies how known OSS vulnerabilities behave when exercised in agent workflows, combining vulnerability-aware semantics, differential execution of vulnerable and fixed software, and multi-layer runtime provenance. The approach distinguishes realized vulnerability effects and identifies the furthest layer they reach across diverse scenarios. Applied to documented workflows in a real-world agent framework, it uncovers several security effects originating from known vulnerabilities in its open-source dependencies.

entry.title: Lightweight drone-mounted 5G base stations: a reproducible OAI testbed on common ARM hardware
entry.summary: Toward Lightweight Aerial 5G gNBs: Reproducible OAI Testbed on Commodity ARM Platforms arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 The paper studies a drone-carried 5G base station in which the core network and central unit stay on the ground, and only the backhaul endpoint, distributed unit, and radio are airborne. Tests with Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Orin Nano as distributed units show Jetson keeping 88.4% of x86 split-DU Ethernet downlink throughput. The authors also release an OAI patch that sends emergency PWS warnings from the central unit to the distributed unit over F1 for reproduction.

entry.title: Hidden Risks of Jev: A Study of Its Security, Privacy, and Dual-Use Concerns
entry.summary: Hidden Risks of Jev: An Empirical Study of Security, Privacy, and Dual Use arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper studies security and privacy risks when Jev, a system that turns natural-language questions into typed answers, is used as a decision layer in applications. Using the official Jev API and a local model, NanoJev, the authors test prompt injection, backdoors from training data poisoning, and attacks that recover sensitive information from constrained outputs. They also evaluate Jev's use in detection tasks and misuse scenarios, finding it remains vulnerable to these threats while its decision capability can serve both beneficial and malicious purposes.

entry.title: Runtime Authorization for Self-Generated Subgoals in Long-Horizon AI Agents
entry.summary: Runtime Authorization of Self-Generated Subgoals in Long-Horizon Tool-Using AI Agents arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper examines how long-horizon AI agents that create their own subgoals, replan, and delegate work can stay within the task a principal approved, which per-tool permission checks alone cannot ensure. The authors propose version-bound witnesses for each goal-graph change and recheck every protected effect at an atomic commit boundary. In 96 matched cases, the complete mechanism committed no forbidden states in 48 drifted cases and completed all 48 benign counterparts. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes runtime authorization for self-generated subgoals in long-horizon tool-using agents, with formal proofs in finite domains and matched-case experiments reporting blocked drift.

entry.title: Static bootstrap placement for encrypted language model decoding
entry.summary: Static Bootstrap Placement for Encrypted Language Model Decoding arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper presents AR-HE, a system that runs the full text-generation loop on a server under homomorphic encryption, selecting each token and writing its embedding back into the encrypted state. The client sends one prompt and waits for the output. A single rule without search places all bootstraps, and the schedule skips unneeded work, packs shared bootstraps, and caches encrypted keys and values. On one NVIDIA H100, the authors report GPT-2 small generating a token in 544 seconds, down from 4715 seconds without optimization.

entry.title: WLPA: A framework for allocating scarce quantum-safe link protection based on the weakest link
entry.summary: WLPA: A Network Management Framework for Allocating Scarce Quantum-Safe Link Postures under Weakest-Link Exposure arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 The paper addresses how network operators can allocate limited quantum-safe protection, such as quantum key distribution, which is hardware-scarce and costly, across links in a network. It presents WLPA, an algorithm that assigns postures under hardware, latency, and compliance constraints, based on the idea that a distributed job's security is set by its weakest active link. The authors identify when common per-link heuristics match the optimum and when they fail, and report validation across 19 experiments.

entry.title: Bounded Reasoning: Comparing Humans and AI in Cyber Defense
entry.summary: Bounded Reasoning: Cognitive Hierarchy in Human-versus-AI Cyber Defense arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper studies a sequential cyber-defense game on an attack graph, where human or reinforcement-learning (DQN) defenders protect cloud assets against a DQN attacker. It compares four defender settings using 80 Mechanical Turk participants and matched automated simulations. Human defenders were more likely to reselect a node after a successful defense than after a failure, while automated defenders did not show this asymmetry. The authors argue that averaged task scores can hide these behavioral differences.

entry.title: Invisible Ink, Visible Lies: Why Watermarking Can Make AI Chatbots Invent Facts
entry.summary: Invisible Ink, Visible Lies: How Production Watermarking Causes LLMs to Hallucinate arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper studies how text watermarks, which help identify AI-generated content, can reduce factual accuracy. In a retrieval-augmented setting where the correct evidence is present, six watermarking methods still produced watermark-induced hallucinations. The authors attribute this to token-level perturbations and attention drift during decoding, and propose two plug-in interventions that reduce factual errors by about 90% relative to watermark-only decoding at a matched detection rate. ★★★★ Notable: The first systematic study of watermark-induced hallucination: under controlled RAG settings, the authors report that six watermarking methods introduce factual errors even when evidence is in context

entry.title: Hardware-accelerated function secret sharing secure against malicious parties (VIGOR-DFA)
entry.summary: Trusted Hardware Acceleration for Malicious-Secure Function Secret Sharing arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper presents VIGOR-DFA, a trusted hardware accelerator for function secret sharing (FSS), a primitive used in two-party private inference and private information retrieval. It adds mechanisms, including a fresh authentication step, a freeze-before-challenge output check, and a one-time resource ledger with a release guard, to resist tampering and replay by a malicious host or GPU. The authors prove static malicious security with abort in a protected-module model and compare against a dealer-based malicious FSS, reporting latency and energy gains along with the cost of malicious security.

entry.title: Predicting cyberattacks using news and podcast data analyzed by AI language models
entry.summary: Forecasting Cybersecurity Incidents Using Geopolitical Data and Large Language Models arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper forecasts cybersecurity incidents by using geopolitical information from news articles and transcribed podcasts, which large language models convert into representations. A classifier trained on past incidents then predicts future ones. On a dataset of over 15,700 records, geopolitical data alone reached 71.4% ROC AUC. Combined with network measurements, it reached 81.3%, above the 77.5% of the prior network-only method.

entry.title: Tracing AI-generated synthetic DNA with a hidden, position-independent watermark
entry.summary: Tracing model-generated DNA with position-independent watermarking arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 Genomic language models can generate synthetic DNA with no record of its origin. The authors embed the SynthID tournament watermark in two such models, Carbon and GENERator-v2, and the detector searches both strands, all start positions and four window lengths, correcting for this multiple search. On a held-out cohort of 1,544 prompts, all 3,088 marked sequences per model were detected, including unedited sequences and those with one substituted, inserted or deleted base. The results show statistical detection only, not biological function, secret-key security, or robustness against an editor who knows the detector.

entry.title: Indistinguishability lifting for keyed oracles and compressed ideal ciphers
entry.summary: Indistinguishability Lifting for Keyed Oracles, Compressed Ideal Cipher, and More Applications arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper proves a general lifting theorem: if two base oracles are indistinguishable under quantum queries, their keyed versions are too, losing only an O(q^2) factor in distinguishing advantage, where q is the number of queries. The authors use this to extend Carolan's compressed permutation oracle into an efficiently implementable compressed ideal cipher, proving preimage resistance of the Davies-Meyer compression function in the quantum ideal cipher model. They also present a modular construction that doubles the message length of any quantum-secure strong pseudorandom permutation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a generic quantum indistinguishability lifting theorem with O(q^2) loss, tight per their claim, and apply it to a compressed ideal cipher and Davies-Meyer preimage resistance.

entry.title: When Talk Isn't Code: Comparing LLM Agents That Simulate and Develop Software
entry.summary: When Talk Isn't Code: Comparing LLM Agents That Simulate and Develop Software arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper compares two ways large language models are used with network protocols: simulating an implementation in conversation and writing the actual program. The authors test 15 models on four protocol implementations using one attack suite. They find that simulation can serve as a first filter but cannot replace testing the generated code.

entry.title: StegoMemory: Agent Memory as a Hidden Covert Channel
entry.summary: StegoMemory: Agentic Memory Acts as Covert Steganographic Channel arXiv · Oct 4, 2026 This paper red-teams AI agents to test whether their memory can secretly carry attacker-chosen strings from one session to another. Across 14,000 attack trials using seven steganographic encoding schemes, about 20.1% of trials recovered the exact hidden payload. Many of these covert transmissions also passed task-completion scoring and safety oversight. The authors conclude that memory integrity and information-flow control should be explicit security requirements for agentic systems.

entry.title: Quantum machine learning to detect hidden attacks on military quantum key distribution
entry.summary: Quantum Machine Learning Protection of Military Quantum Key Distribution Against Cryptographically Camouflaged Attacks arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 The paper studies implementation attacks on military quantum key distribution, where an adversary with a hidden backdoor in a generator hides attacked blocks within honest noise. Detection is shown to reduce to a discrete logarithm problem, which a quantum kernel using Shor's algorithm can solve. In simulations on the Ghillie decoy-state BB84 simulator, the quantum kernel scores 1.000 on camouflaged attacks while classical monitors score 0.458 to 0.516.

entry.title: The Same Zero: Why Identical Attack Success Rates May Mean Different Guarantees for LLM-Agent Defenses
entry.summary: The Same Zero: Why Identical ASR Can Imply Different Guarantees in LLM-Agent Security arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 The paper applies Verification Autonomy Levels (VAL, L0 to L5) to classify 22 LLM-agent security defenses by what guarantee they provide and where it comes from. Under equal budget, it compares a VAL-guided defense stack with a common intuition-based stack across 50 scenarios, 12 attack variants, and testbeds including AgentDojo and JADE. The authors conclude that a zero attack success rate is an outcome rather than a guarantee, since identical zeros can arise from very different sources.

entry.title: Verifying Audited Proprietary Software Without Revealing Its Code
entry.summary: Attestable Audit: Property-Based Attestation for Proprietary Workloads without Artifact Disclosure arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 The paper proposes an architecture that combines two TEE-based workloads, attestable build and attestable audit, so a verifier can confirm that a running program was built from source code meeting audited properties. Audit verdicts are bound to the source code digest, so neither the source code nor the build artifact needs to be disclosed. A proof-of-concept on Intel SGX with Gramine runs the Bandit analyzer on Python code to demonstrate practicality.

entry.title: Reactivating Alignment: Intention-Aware Input-Output Matching to Defend LLMs from Jailbreaks
entry.summary: Reactivating Alignment: Defending LLMs from Jailbreaks via Intention-Aware Input-Output Matching arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper presents SENTINEL, a plug-and-play defense that works during generation to block jailbreak attacks on large language models. It treats the problem as extracting the attacker's true intent, using the fact that instruction-tuned models' outputs tend to align semantically with that intent. SENTINEL matches aligned input-output regions, scores them with refusal-direction projections, and halts generation when needed. On HarmBench, it reduces jailbreak success rates to close to 5% while keeping over-refusal low.

entry.title: Guess My Weight: Recovering Exact Float32 Neural-Network Weights via Power Side Channels
entry.summary: Guess My Weight: Profiled Side-Channel Recovery of Floating-Point Neural-Network Weights arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper studies whether floating-point neural-network weights on embedded devices can be recovered bit-for-bit from power side-channel leakage during inference. The authors propose a profiled template attack that targets the multiplication of a known input with a first-layer weight, using a hierarchical coarse-to-fine search over the 32-bit candidate space. Experiments on a ChipWhisperer-Lite with an Arm Cortex-M4 report a 99% bit-exact success rate with 171 traces and 100% from 263 traces onward.

entry.title: Large Language Models and Augmented Democracy: Studying LLM Digital Twins for Representing Citizen and Party Preferences and Their Vulnerability to Attacks
entry.summary: Large Language Models and Augmented Democracy arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This thesis examines large language model (LLM)-based digital twins as intermediaries in augmented democracy. Using Brazilian online experiment data, it tests whether personalized twins can predict citizens' preferences on unseen policy proposals. Using Swiss parliamentary records, it builds party-level twins from lawmaker agents and checks whether their deliberation captures more intra-party views than official communications. It also studies prompt-injection attacks on LLM-mediated deliberation using UK 2023 experiment data and evaluates a defensive pipeline.

entry.title: JASPER: Joint Reliability and Security Assessment for Split Computing at the Edge
entry.summary: JASPER: Special Session on Joint Reliability And Security Assessment of SPlit Computing for Edge Robustness arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper presents a unified framework for jointly evaluating the reliability and security of Split Computing, where deep neural network inference is divided between edge devices and cloud servers. Reliability is measured with neuron-level fault injection using Mean Relative Accuracy Degradation, and security with feature-map-aware adversarial attacks using Attack Success Rate. Tests on ten ResNet-50 configurations show MRAD of 44.3% to 61.2% and attack success rates up to 98.8%, with joint metrics revealing vulnerabilities hidden by separate analysis.

entry.title: A cheat-sensitive routing method that hides destinations in quantum networks
entry.summary: A Cheat-Sensitive Primitive for Destination-Private Quantum Routing arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 Intermediate nodes in quantum networks distribute entanglement but may learn which users are connected. The paper proposes a minimal two-call routing primitive in which Alice links with one of several clients while testing whether the provider Bob has disturbed a coherently encoded request. The construction adapts the hidden-order mechanism of quantum private queries and uses a private matching qubit held by the selected client. It detects an explicit destination-reading attack with nonzero probability, but does not yet give a quantitative information-disturbance tradeoff or composable security.[]

entry.title: GrayShield: Bit-Level Sanitization to Protect Transformer Models in the AI Supply Chain
entry.summary: GrayShield: Bit-Level Sanitization for Transformer Model Supply-Chain Security arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 The paper notes that the least significant bits of 32-bit floating-point weights in Transformer models such as BERT and ViT can be misused as covert channels to hide malicious payloads. The authors propose GrayShield, a lightweight, post-training, data-free method that overwrites this mantissa-LSB channel with a Gray-code-guided low-transition sequence. Tested on four model presets and two real malware payloads, it keeps accuracy impact below 1% and reduces recovery by about 49.96 percentage points under five attacker variants.

entry.title: Modeling How Users' Deletion Requests Can Shape Machine Unlearning Outcomes
entry.summary: Modeling Deletion Requests in Machine Unlearning arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper examines how users exercising the "right to erasure" might influence AI model behavior through machine unlearning. It defines two user behaviors when requesting data deletion, adaptivity and collectivity, and theoretically compares groups that do and do not display them using results from stochastic optimization. The authors also show how data valuation techniques can be used to design deletion requesters that significantly alter model behavior, and their computer vision experiments examine the differential effects of these behaviors.

entry.title: CyTReX: An Explainable AI Framework for Threat Reasoning in DER Networks
entry.summary: CyTReX: Explainable AI-Based Cybersecurity Threat Reasoning Framework for DER Networks arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper presents CyTReX, a framework that turns anomaly alerts from distributed energy resource networks into ranked threat hypotheses for security analysts. It constrains large language model reasoning with a structured evidence packet combining detection outputs, SHAP feature attributions, surrogate rules, and threat intelligence. Each hypothesis is meant to trace back to explicit evidence, and incomplete or conflicting evidence is reported. Evaluation across five configurations shows the complete pipeline gives the richest evidence-grounded reasoning context.

entry.title: Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Teaching AI Agents to Resist Prompt Injection Attacks
entry.summary: Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper proposes Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning (SRFT), a training method that helps language model agents learn from their own failures under adversarial conditions. Instead of only imitating expert behavior, agents are shown compromised trajectories created by injected attacks, and an expert model generates reasoning that contrasts unsafe and optimal actions. The authors implement this as SR-Agent on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, and report reduced attack success rates on static and adaptive benchmarks while preserving task performance.

entry.title: Autonomous Active Directory Attacks via a Multi-Model Harness: A NeuroSploit Benchmark on GOAD
entry.summary: Autonomous Active Directory Exploitation via Multi-Model Harness Orchestration: A Benchmark Study with NeuroSploit on GOAD arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper benchmarks NeuroSploit v4.2.0, an open-source Rust autonomous pentest harness, against GOAD, a deliberately vulnerable multi-forest Active Directory lab. The harness uses 22 AD-specific agents and 7 multi-stage attack-chain playbooks spanning enumeration through cross-forest trust abuse. It is compared with direct large-language-model invocation, and the authors report 96–100% technique coverage for the harness versus 21–54% for direct invocation.

entry.title: Learning to Watermark Speech Synthesis Against Reconstruction Attacks
entry.summary: Learning to Watermark Speech Synthesis Against Model-Driven Reconstruction arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper proposes Thrive, a multi-bit generative watermarking framework for modern autoregressive text-to-speech systems, designed to trace synthesized speech back to the requesting user. The authors find that no single watermark carrier stays reliable across reconstruction models, so Thrive combines Rise, which injects watermarks into intermediate representations, with Care, which selects waveform or spectral experts per bit. Experiments report 87.6% average recovery accuracy under reconstruction attacks, with source attribution supported over candidate sets of up to 10,000 identities.

entry.title: Rethinking watermark teachers for language model fingerprinting
entry.summary: Language Model Fingerprinting Requires Rethinking Watermark Teachers arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper examines LLM fingerprinting, which embeds a statistical watermark into model weights so owners can identify their models behind black-box APIs. The authors find that a recent protocol's utility evaluation understates text quality loss in open-ended generation. They propose near-tie restriction, which limits watermark bias to tokens close to the base model's top prediction, improving the trade-off between detectability and text quality.

entry.title: Encrypted Statistical Modeling with Fully Homomorphic Encryption in R
entry.summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption for Statistical Modeling arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper shows how two R packages, openfhe.R and homomorpheR, enable statistical analyses on encrypted data so multiple parties can jointly model without sharing raw records. Validation studies cover distributed stratified Cox regression and federated Cox-lasso using consensus ADMM, where only the cross-site update is encrypted. The parties are assumed honest-but-curious, and threshold key generation is used.

entry.title: From Temporary Access to Persistent Surveillance: Matter Smart Home Security Risks
entry.summary: From Temporary Access to Persistent Surveillance: Why Matter Matters in Smart Homes arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper examines Matter, an open smart home standard that uses cryptography for device authentication and data confidentiality, and how its openness exposes protocol and implementation details. The authors show that an attacker with temporary physical access can exploit design and implementation flaws to extract credentials and impersonate devices, maintaining surveillance and control after leaving. A proof-of-concept on a simulated smart home with commercial devices and development boards validates the attack, and four mitigation strategies are proposed.

entry.title: How gradients add to text leakage in split language models, counted per token and per document
entry.summary: What Gradients Add to Text Leakage in Split Language Models, Counted per Token and per Document arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 The paper shows that in split learning for language models, an observer can rebuild most of a client's text from the activations sent to the server and the gradients returned. On GPT-2, an attacker recovers 94.20% of tokens from activations alone and 97.38% with gradients, while exact recovery of 32-token documents rises from 13.71% to 37.77%. The authors recommend reporting leakage both per token and per document, and treating what a split model transmits as sensitive as the original text. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that gradients returned by the server raise text leakage in split learning: on GPT-2, per-token recovery rises from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact per-document recovery from 13.71% to 3

entry.title: Privacy audit of synthetic gene expression data using a unified weighted-distance attack framework
entry.summary: Auditing the Privacy of Synthetic Gene Expression Data: A Unified Weighted-Distance Framework for No-Box Membership Inference arXiv · Oct 3, 2026 This paper red-teams synthetic gene expression data derived from TCGA bulk RNA-seq, released by the ELSA Health 2026 Challenge, by testing membership inference attacks. The authors unify five no-box attacks in one weighted-distance framework that differs only in how genes are weighted. Against a conditional variational autoencoder, spectral residualization raised pan-cancer TCGA AUC from 0.8251 to 0.8951 and TPR at 1% FPR from 0.3842 to 0.5970. Biological pathway priors did not transfer across targets.
